posts.content: Alexandre BALMES View Alexandre BALMES’ profile • 3rd+ CTO & Staff Architect | Ingénierie de systèmes robustes pour l’IA | Expert DDD & Architecture Logicielle 2d • 2d Visible to everyone En tant que dev ou responsable technique, on fait tous face au même constat avec les LLM : c'est un gain de temps phénoménal mais cela manque souvent de déterminisme et de contrôle. C'est pour répondre à ce besoin de maîtrise que j'ai développé AWF (AI Workflow Framework). Après l'avoir éprouvé sur mes propres projets, je rends l'outil accessible à tous. Le concept n'est pas de proposer un énième "claw", mais un binaire en Go permettant d'orchestrer vos agents IA (Claude, Gemini, Codex) via des workflows YAML structurés. Pourquoi cette approche : - Déterminisme : on sort du "prompt and pray". On définit des étapes, des conditions, des boucles et une gestion d'erreurs. Comme avec Ansible, ça marche ou ça casse. - Agnosticisme : ne soyez pas prisonnier d'un seul modèle. Vous pouvez switcher entre Claude Code, Gemini ou OpenAI au sein d'un même workflow. - Approche professionnelle : gestion du parallélisme, audit trail, support XDG. C'est un outil conçu par un développeur pour ceux qui maîtrisent leur ligne de commande et AWF s'auto-développe désormais via ses propres workflows. Le repo est ouvert et les retours sont les bienvenus pour ceux qui souhaitent industrialiser leurs interactions avec l'IA. https://lnkd.in/eQr6xgHZ GitHub - awf-project/cli: A Go CLI tool for orchestrating AI agents through YAML workflows github.com

posts.content: Benjamin Tardy View Benjamin Tardy’s profile • 2nd AI & ML Engineer 1w • 1w Visible to everyone L'évolution des architectures LLM en une seule page ! Sebastian Raschka maintient une "LLM Architecture Gallery" qui compile les fiches techniques d'architecture de 42 modèles, de GPT-2 aux dernières sorties de début 2026. En parcourant l'ensemble, quelques tendances sautent aux yeux : → Le Mixture-of-Experts est devenu la norme pour les gros modèles. → DeepSeek V3 est devenu le blueprint de l'industrie. Son combo MLA + MoE sparse + dense prefix a été repris presque tel quel par Mistral Large 3 (qualifié explicitement de "near-clone" dans la galerie), Kimi K2. GLM-4.5 s'en inspire également. → L'attention hybride émerge comme la prochaine frontière. Les modèles les plus récents commencent à remplacer une partie des couches d'attention classique par des mécanismes linéaires. L'objectif : garder la qualité du Transformer tout en réduisant le coût sur les longs contextes. → Les fenêtres de contexte ont explosé. On est passé de 1 024 tokens (GPT-2) à 128K en standard, avec des modèles à 1M tokens. La galerie est même disponible en poster haute résolution, la version 2026 du poster des 151 Pokémon de Kanto qu'on avait au mur de notre chambre sauf qu'ici c'est 42 architectures LLM avec leurs fiches techniques. _______ 📬 Veille Data/IA toutes les semaines – 15 min chrono : humanframework.substack(.)com Je publie 3x par semaine sur l'IA, le machine learning et la data en général.

Et ça casse votre code en production. Le problème est simple. Cursor, Claude Code ou même OpenCode sont puissants. Mais ils ne comprennent pas la structure de votre codebase. Votre agent modifie une fonction. Sauf qu'il ne sait pas que 47 autres fonctions en dépendent. Résultat : des breaking changes livrées en prod. (ou jusqu'à 5x plus de token consommés pour trouver les bugs, les typing qui ont sautés etc) GitNexus change la donne. C'est un outil open source qui transforme n'importe quelle codebase en knowledge graph. Chaque dépendance, chaque chaîne d'appels, chaque flux d'exécution est mappé. Concrètement, il expose 7 outils à vos agents via MCP : 1. Impact analysis : visualiser le blast radius avant de toucher une fonction 2. Process-grouped search : retrouver du code par flux métier, pas juste par mot-clé 3. Context 360 : voir tout ce qui appelle, importe ou étend un symbole 4. Detect changes : analyser le risque d'un diff avant le commit 5. Rename multi-fichiers : renommer un symbole partout, en confiance 6. Cypher queries : interroger le graphe directement 7. List repos : gérer plusieurs repos indexés Le plus impressionnant : → Même les petits modèles deviennent fiables parce que le graphe fait le gros du travail → Tout tourne en local, aucun code envoyé sur un serveur → 12 langages supportés dont Python, TypeScript, Go, Rust, Java → Un seul serveur MCP sert tous vos repos indexés Avant : votre agent faisait 4 à 10 requêtes pour comprendre une fonction. Maintenant : une seule requête, contexte complet. Arrêtez de laisser vos agents coder sans carte. Donnez-leur le plan complet. --- 🚀 Pour devenir AI Engineer, maîtrisez : Software Engineering, System Design, Machine Learning et LLM Engineering. posts.title: Maxime Labonne View Maxime Labonne’s profile • 2nd Head of Post-Training @ Liquid AI 3w • 3w Visible to everyone 🧲 Doc-t
posts.content: Maxime Labonne View Maxime Labonne’s profile • 2nd Head of Post-Training @ Liquid AI 3w • 3w Visible to everyone 🧲 Doc-to-LoRA: Turning documents to adapters! Long contexts are expensive. Every RAG system, every cached system prompt, every user preference file sitting in a context window is burning memory and adding latency. Context distillation is the principled fix, but it requires gradient updates per document, making it impractical for anything interactive or personalized. This paper takes a clean shot at the problem: → Instead of fine-tuning the LLM per document, they train a hypernetwork (Doc-to-LoRA) that reads a document once and outputs a LoRA adapter in a single forward pass, no backprop needed. → The hypernetwork uses a Perceiver-style cross-attention module, mapping variable-length token activations to a fixed-rank LoRA. Long docs are chunked and adapters are concatenated along the rank dimension, enabling generalization beyond the training context length. → On NIAH, D2L trained on 256-token sequences generalizes near-perfectly to 40K tokens at test time. Inference memory stays under 50MB regardless of haystack size, versus 12+ GB for the KV-cache baseline. → On SQuAD, D2L reaches ~82% of ICL performance with sub-second internalization latency and under 2GB VRAM, while vanilla CD needs 100+ seconds and 40+ GB. → A surprising zero-shot result: D2L transfers visual information from a VLM into a text-only LLM through adapter generation, with no explicit multimodal training. The approach is genuinely compelling, but the evaluation could be improved. Experiments use the (extremely) outdated Gemma-2-2B as the base model almost exclusively. We have no idea if the hypernetwork generalizes across different base architectures, or if training a new Doc-to-LoRA per model family kills the practical appeal. What I really want to see: can Doc-to-LoRA handle system prompt internalization robustly enough to replace static context in production deployments? Happy to hear your thoughts!

posts.title: Benjamin Tardy View Benjamin Tardy’s profile • 2nd AI & ML Engineer 2w • 2w Visible to everyone La plupart des équipes p
posts.content: Benjamin Tardy View Benjamin Tardy’s profile • 2nd AI & ML Engineer 2w • 2w Visible to everyone La plupart des équipes paient 4x trop cher pour leurs embeddings sans vraiment le savoir. Quand on a besoin d'embeddings le réflexe c'est de prendre text-embedding-ada-002 ou text-embedding-3-large à 1536 dimensions (voir plus). La logique derrière semble imparable : plus de dimensions = meilleure qualité. Mais la réalité est plus nuancée que cela. → Calculer la similarité cosine entre vecteurs à 384 dims est plus rapide qu'à 1536. → Stocker 10M vecteurs à 384 dims coûte moins cher (beaucoup) qu'à 1536. Et sur la majorité des use cases classiques (support client, knowledge base interne, documentation technique standard) : la différence de qualité de retrieval mesurée est très marginale. Pourquoi ça marche quand même avec des embeddings plus petits ? Grâce à Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL). L'idée : entraîner le modèle de façon à ce que les premières dimensions condensent l'essentiel de la sémantique, les dimensions suivantes ne faisant qu'affiner, d'où l'image des poupées russes. Ainsi, un vecteur de 256 dims tiré d'un modèle MRL est aussi précis qu'un vecteur de 1536 dims d'une ancienne génération de modèles. OpenAI l'a intégré dans text-embedding-3, Nomic dans nomic-embed-text etc... En revanche il existe toujours des cas où les grandes dimensions restent intéressantes : → Documentation avec des variations de nomenclature très subtiles → Corpus multilingues denses → Bases hétérogènes où des faux positifs de similarité apparaissent à basse dimension Pour la grande majorité des cas vous pouvez commencer à 384. Mesurez, observez et tentez avec de plus grandes dimensions si les résultats ne vous semblent pas satisfaisants mais ne faites pas l'erreur de prendre les plus grandes dims sans tester les plus petites. _______ 📬 Veille Data/IA toutes les semaines – 15 min chrono : lebriefia.substack(.)com Je publie 3x par semaine sur l'IA, le machine learning et la data en général.

posts.content: Lan Chu View Lan Chu’s profile • 2nd AI Tech Lead | Senior Data Scientist | Work with LLMs before they were cool 3w • 3w Visible to everyone Remember our good friend BM25 that empowers every RAG hybrid search? We all know it is powerful but do you know how BM25 works exactly? It is a term-based retrieval method that improves upon TF-IDF, addressing issues with 𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐦 𝐬𝐚𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐝𝐨𝐜𝐮𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐥𝐞𝐧𝐠𝐭𝐡. 1. 𝐓𝐞𝐫𝐦 𝐒𝐚𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 (𝐤1 𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐚𝐦𝐞𝐭𝐞𝐫) If a document contains 100 occurrences of the term “computer,” is it twice as relevant as a document that contains 50 occurrences? Probably not. BM25 uses k1 to control diminishing returns. As term frequency increases, the score saturates, meaning additional occurrences contribute less and less to relevance. This prevents keyword stuffing from artificially inflating scores. 2. 𝐃𝐨𝐜𝐮𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐋𝐞𝐧𝐠𝐭𝐡 𝐍𝐨𝐫𝐦𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐳𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 (𝐛 𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐚𝐦𝐞𝐭𝐞𝐫) If a document is very short and it contains “computer” once, that might already be a good indicator of relevance. But if the document is long and the term “computer” only appears once, it is likely that the document is not about computers. Long documents are more likely to contain many relevant terms, without making the document itself more relevant, leading to false positives. We want to give a reward to term matches to short documents and penalize the long ones. But what defines if a document is a short or a long one? BM25 uses the average corpus length (dl_avg) as a reference point. Documents longer than this average are considered long, while those shorter are considered short documents. → Short documents get rewarded for term matches → Long documents get penalized → The b parameter controls how strong this effect is. The higher the value of b, the higher the penalty for large documents. These two simple mechanisms make BM25 incredibly fasat and effective at finding relevant documents, which is why it is still the backbone of many modern retrieval systems. Are there other term-based retrieval methods that you are using?

(Boris Cherny, the head of Claude Code, just revealed his exact workflow) Follow these 6 steps. ↓ Most engineers use Claude Code like a chatbot. They prompt one session and wait. You can run 10 to 15 sessions in parallel and ship code simultaneously instead. 1/ Set Up Parallel Sessions -Terminal: Run 5 Claude Code sessions simultaneously in your terminal -Web: Run 5 to 10 additional sessions in the browser at the same time -Combined: Every session works on a different task while you focus elsewhere 2/ Build Your CLAUDE.md File -Self-improvement loop: After every correction, Claude updates its own rules so the mistake never happens again -Lessons file: All rules live in tasks/lessons.md and are reviewed at the start of every session -The command: "After every correction, end with: Update your CLAUDE.md so you don't make that mistake again" 3/ Set Workflow Orchestration Rules -Plan Node Default: Enter plan mode for any task with 3 or more steps before writing a single line -Subagent Strategy: Offload research, exploration, and parallel analysis to subagents to keep main context clean -Verification Before Done: Never mark a task complete without proving it works first 4/ Structure Every Task in 3 Parts -Part 1: Write plan to tasks/todo.md with checkable items before starting -Part 2: Execute with high-level summary at each step, mark items complete as you go -Part 3: Add review section to tasks/todo.md and update tasks/lessons.md after corrections 5/ Set Core Principles -Simplicity First: Make every change as simple as possible, minimal code impact -No Laziness: Find root causes, no temporary fixes, senior developer standards -Minimal Impact: Changes should only touch what is necessary, never introduce bugs 6/ Delegate Entire Problem Types -SQL: Boris has not written a single line of SQL in 6 months, Claude pulls BigQuery data directly via CLI -Bug fixing: When given a bug report, Claude fixes it autonomously, zero context switching required -CI tests: Claude fixes failing tests without being told how This is just one way to use Claude Code the way its builder actually uses it. posts.title: Adham Sersour View Adham Sersour’s profile • 1st Senior AI/ML Engineer 3w • 3w Visible to everyone The next trillion-dol
posts.content: Adham Sersour View Adham Sersour’s profile • 1st Senior AI/ML Engineer 3w • 3w Visible to everyone The next trillion-dollar AI company probably won't build a chatbot. It will build a model that can see your kitchen, hear "clean up," and physically do it. That model already exists, it worked in real apartments last year, and the architecture behind it is surprisingly simple to understand. I'll be honest, when I first stumbled on the term "VLA" a few months ago, I thought it was yet another acronym the AI hype machine invented to sound smart. Vision-Language-Action models. Sounds like something someone puts on a slide deck to justify a $600 million funding round. Then I actually dug into the research and something clicked, because VLAs represent the clearest progression I've seen in AI right now, and almost nobody outside the robotics community is paying attention. Here's what rewired my thinking. Your LLM is a brain in a jar. It can reason, plan, and compose, but it has no eyes, no hands, and no body. It lives entirely in the world of text. Researchers fixed this in two steps: first they gave it eyes (vision encoders that project images into the same token space the LLM already understands), and then they gave it hands (action outputs that generate motor commands from what it sees and hears). That's the LLM → VLM → VLA progression in one paragraph. A brain, then a brain that sees, then a brain that sees and acts in the physical world. Now here's where it gets interesting: the field can't agree on how to represent physical actions. One camp (Google's RT-2, OpenVLA) discretizes robot movements into tokens, same vocabulary trick as language. The other camp (Physical Intelligence's π₀) argues actions should stay continuous and uses flow matching to generate smooth trajectories directly. Both work, and the most interesting research right now is happening at their intersection. What made me take this seriously wasn't the tech demos though, it was the investment signals. Physical Intelligence raised $600M in their Series B, VLA papers at ICLR went from 9 to 164 in one year (that's 18×), and π₀.5 was tested in completely unseen San Francisco homes last April, not labs, actual apartments it had never seen, and it worked. The pattern underneath VLAs (extend a foundation model to new modalities and new output types) is the same pattern powering AI agents today. If you're building systems that take actions in digital environments, you're solving a version of the same architectural problem. I wrote a deeper breaking down the architecture, the two camps, and why the numbers say this is real and not hype. Link in comments. 5 resources if you want to go hands-on: → OpenVLA (open-source 7B, beat Google's 55B RT-2-X) → π₀ (open-sourced by Physical Intelligence) → NVIDIA GR00T N1 (humanoid VLA foundation model) → Open X-Embodiment (1M+ real robot trajectories, 34 labs) → HuggingFace LeRobot (the framework to start with) → UnifoLM-VLA — Unitree, open-source, built for the G1 → VLA 2.0 — XPeng, shared across robots, cars and drones on the same model

posts.title: Shubham Saboo View Shubham Saboo’s profile • 3rd+ Senior AI Product Manager @ Google | Awesome LLM Apps (#1 AI Agents Gi
posts.content: Shubham Saboo View Shubham Saboo’s profile • 3rd+ Senior AI Product Manager @ Google | Awesome LLM Apps (#1 AI Agents GitHub repo with 103k+ stars) | 3x AI Author | Community of 350k+ AI developers | Views are my Own 3w • 3w Visible to everyone This open-source project just made vector databases optional for RAG 🤯 No embeddings. No chunking. No similarity search. Meet PageIndex, a vectorless, reasoning-based RAG system that retrieves like a human expert. It just hit 98.7% accuracy on FinanceBench, outperforming traditional vector RAG by a significant margin. Vector search finds what's semantically similar, but similarity is not relevance. When you're working with financial reports, legal filings, or technical manuals, you need reasoning, multi-step logic, and context across sections. A similarity score can't give you that. PageIndex thinks differently. It reads your document and builds a hierarchical tree index, like a table of contents but optimized for how LLMs actually think. Then it reasons through that tree to find what's actually relevant, the same way a human expert flips through a 200-page annual report. What that looks like in practice: • Documents stay in their natural structure, no artificial chunking • The LLM navigates the tree using reasoning, not pattern matching • Every answer comes with page and section references • No opaque embeddings, no "vibe retrieval" Works on SEC filings, legal documents, technical manuals, and academic papers. Anything that needs precision and exceeds your context window. Vector database RAG was the best we had. This is what we actually needed. Link to the GitHub repo in the comments.

posts.content: Sumanth P View Sumanth P’s profile • 3rd+ Machine Learning Developer Advocate | LLMs, AI Agents & RAG | Shipping Open Source AI Apps | AI Engineering 1mo • 1mo Visible to everyone Fine-tune LLM agents without fine-tuning LLMs! Memento is a memory based continual learning framework for LLM agents that lets them learn from experience over time without touching model weights. It maintains a Case Bank of past trajectories including tasks, step sequences, tool usage, and outcomes. When a new task comes in, the agent plans and acts by pulling from similar past cases instead of starting from zero. Memento follows a planner and executor setup: 1. The Planner (an LLM) breaks the task into subtasks, retrieves relevant cases, and chooses a plan. 2. The Executor runs those subtasks using tools like search, code execution, or document processing through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), then logs the results back into memory. Key Features: • Memory based continual learning that improves agents through stored experience • Planner and executor architecture with case based reasoning for task decomposition • Unified tool ecosystem for search, code execution, document processing, media analysis and more • Learning without weight updates by retrieving and reusing relevant past cases • Strong results on long horizon and out of distribution tasks in reported benchmarks It is 100% open source. posts.title: Lan Chu View Lan Chu’s profile • 2nd AI Tech Lead | Senior Data Scientist | Work with LLMs before they were cool 1mo • 1
posts.content: Lan Chu View Lan Chu’s profile • 2nd AI Tech Lead | Senior Data Scientist | Work with LLMs before they were cool 1mo • 1mo Visible to everyone Want to level up your post-training skills? ⬇️ Finetuning has become much more accessible with Unsloth. I finetuned a 20B parameter model gpt-oss in 1h30 minutes on a free GPU. 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐬𝐞𝐭𝐮𝐩 • Model: OpenAI GPT-OSS 20B • Hardware: Free Colab T4 with 16GB VRAM • Technique: 4-bit quantization + LoRA adapters (rank=8) • Finetuning time: 90 minutes for 1 full epoch Unsloth is an optimization layer that works with HuggingFace Transformers + TRL and pytorch directly. 𝘚𝘢𝘮𝘦 𝘤𝘰𝘥𝘦, 𝘴𝘢𝘮𝘦 𝘮𝘰𝘥𝘦𝘭𝘴, 𝘣𝘶𝘵 2-5𝘹 𝘧𝘢𝘴𝘵𝘦𝘳 𝘸𝘪𝘵𝘩 70% 𝘭𝘦𝘴𝘴 𝘮𝘦𝘮𝘰𝘳𝘺. 𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐦𝐚𝐤𝐞𝐬 𝐔𝐧𝐬𝐥𝐨𝐭𝐡 𝐟𝐚𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐫? Unsloth wrote their own GPU kernels together with a smarter gradient checkpointing implementation that uses ~30% less VRAM than the default. These optimizations apply whether you're doing LoRA or full fine-tuning. I tried running the same setup with pure HuggingFace to compare performance but hit multiple issues. First, gpt-oss is quantized in an MXFP4 format, which doesn't support backpropagation (it is an inference-only format). To train, you need to convert to something like BitsAndBytes NF4. Unsloth handles this conversion automatically. With vanilla HuggingFace, however, the only option is to dequantize back to bf16, which requires 65GB+ VRAM. The free T4 tier doesn’t have that much memory. But even if we try to load Unsloth’s BnB 4-bit version of the model directly with Huggingface, I still ran out of memory. Meaning that even with the same model weights, Unsloth's loading and memory management is much more efficient than pure HuggingFace. If you're experimenting with fine-tuning, Unsloth makes it easier than ever. Below is the 𝗺𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲𝘁𝗲 𝗟𝗟𝗠 𝗳𝗶𝗻𝗲-𝘁𝘂𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗻𝗼𝘁𝗲𝗯𝗼𝗼𝗸 𝗰𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 offering 100+ fine-tuning notebooks for Google Colab, covering a wide range of models like OpenAI, Llama, Qwen, Deepseek, Gemma and more. Check it out and advance your AI skill. Link in comments! ⬇️ I have one question though: Unsloth seems too good to be true. Is there any catch?

posts.title: Nina Fernanda Durán View Nina Fernanda Durán’s profile • 3rd+ AI Architect · Ship AI to production, here’s how 1mo • 1mo
posts.content: Nina Fernanda Durán View Nina Fernanda Durán’s profile • 3rd+ AI Architect · Ship AI to production, here’s how 1mo • 1mo Visible to everyone If your LLM can't connect facts across documents, you are losing context between chunks. Stop retrieving text. Start mapping relationships. Build GraphRAG to link the dots across your data with 3 commands: 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗜𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 Most tools overcomplicate the stack. This framework keeps it lean. ◼︎ Install the engine: pip install cognee ◼︎ Set your environment keys and run the core pipeline: 1️⃣ Ingest your unstructured data await cognee.add("data_source") 2️⃣ Build the knowledge graph await cognee.cognify() 3️⃣ Query the persistent memory results = await cognee·search("How do these concepts relate?")` 𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗯𝗲𝗮𝘁𝘀 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗮𝗿𝗱 𝗩𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗼𝗿 𝗦𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵 Standard RAG treats your data like a pile of shredded paper. You search for a fragment ➨ you get a fragment. This implements an ECL ➨ Extract ➨ Cognify ➨ Load pipeline. It doesn't just store embeddings; it maps relationships. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗧𝗲𝗰𝗵𝗻𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗘𝗱𝗴𝗲: ◼︎ Vector Similarity ↳ Finds the "what" using semantic proximity. ◼︎ Graph Traversal ↳ Finds the "why" and "how" by following entity edges. ◼︎ Hybrid Reasoning ↳ Combines both to answer queries that span multiple documents. The magic happens during the .cognify() step. It isn't just indexing; it's engineering a memory layer. 1️⃣ Entity Extraction ➨ Identifying the "actors" in your text. 2️⃣ Relationship Mapping ➨ Defining how those actors interact. 3️⃣ Semantic Embedding➨ Placing everything in a HD vector space. The API is designed for high-velocity development: .add() The entry point ↳ Handles documents, audio, and text ➨ Prepares the raw buffer. .cognify() The heavy lifter ↳ Generates the Knowledge Graph ➨ Creates the persistent intelligence layer. .search() The retrieval head. ↳ Merges vector search with graph paths. ➨ Delivers high-context results to your Agent. .memify() (Incoming) ↳ Deep semantic enrichment. ➨ Self-evolving memory nodes. Stop building basic search. Start building cognitive memory. ❱❱ Try yourself ❱❱ GitHub link in comments - - - - - 𖤂 Repost to help your network build with AI. I’m Nina. I build with AI and share how it’s done weekly

posts.title: Benjamin Tardy View Benjamin Tardy’s profile • 2nd AI & ML Engineer 1mo • 1mo Visible to everyone Mon agent va envoyer u
posts.content: Benjamin Tardy View Benjamin Tardy’s profile • 2nd AI & ML Engineer 1mo • 1mo Visible to everyone Mon agent va envoyer un mail, mon agent va créer un ticket Jira, il va corriger ma MR. Mais avec quelles permissions ? Quand un agent fait appel à un MCP ou une API, au nom de qui le fait-il ? Avec quel token ? Comment on identifie qui a demandé quoi et à quel agent ? L'un des patterns qui émerge est le On-Behalf-Of (OBO). Au lieu de donner à l'agent vos identifiants et/ou un accès admin, on met en place une chaîne de délégation explicite. Vous autorisez l'agent à agir en votre nom avec des permissions précises, limitées dans le temps, et traçables. Les flows OAuth 2.0 actuels n'ont pas été conçus pour ça. Ils gèrent deux acteurs : un utilisateur et une application. Avec les agents, on passe à trois : l'utilisateur, l'application, et l'agent qui agit. Et c'est pour ça que l'IETF (l'organisme qui standardise les protocoles d'Internet) travaille en ce moment sur une extension OAuth dédiée aux agents IA. Un Internet Draft qui introduit deux nouveaux paramètres : requested_actor pour identifier quel agent demande l'accès, et actor_token pour qu'il prouve son identité lors de l'échange de tokens. Permission discovery, delegation chains, least-privilege, audit trails sont des sujets sur lesquels on peut parier, si vous avez peur que votre métier disparaisse. _______ 📬 Veille Data/IA toutes les semaines – 15 min chrono : lebriefia.substack(.)com Je publie 3x par semaine sur l'IA, le machine learning et la data en général.

posts.title: Avi Pilcer View Avi Pilcer’s profile • 2nd Autonomous AI companies. Zero team. Zero gatekeeping. Shipping daily in publi
posts.content: Avi Pilcer View Avi Pilcer’s profile • 2nd Autonomous AI companies. Zero team. Zero gatekeeping. Shipping daily in public. 1mo • 1mo Visible to everyone 14 agentic coding lessons from the founder of OpenClaw, 🦄 Peter Steinberger. Who sold to OpenAI. I dug through every post on his blog. Ranked by how hard they hit. Save this. ⸻ 𝟭/ 𝗡𝗘𝗔𝗥 𝗖𝗢𝗡𝗧𝗘𝗫𝗧 𝗟𝗜𝗠𝗜𝗧𝗦, 𝗠𝗢𝗗𝗘𝗟𝗦 𝗣𝗔𝗡𝗜𝗖. Raw thinking leaks past 180K tokens. Compact early. Compact often. 𝟮/ "𝗠𝗔𝗡𝗬 𝗦𝗠𝗔𝗟𝗟 𝗕𝗢𝗠𝗕𝗦, 𝗡𝗘𝗩𝗘𝗥 𝗙𝗔𝗧 𝗠𝗔𝗡." Atomic commits. Something breaks? Roll back one commit. Not 40 files. 𝟯/ 𝗧𝗛𝗜𝗡𝗞 𝗙𝗥𝗢𝗠 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗔𝗚𝗘𝗡𝗧'𝗦 𝗣𝗘𝗥𝗦𝗣𝗘𝗖𝗧𝗜𝗩𝗘. It starts at zero. 100K+ lines, no context. I cut my CLAUDE md from 727 to 128 lines. Accuracy jumped. Let instruction files grow organically from real problems. Never architect upfront. 𝟰/ 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗔𝗚𝗘𝗡𝗧𝗜𝗖 𝗧𝗥𝗔𝗣 Stage 1: short prompts. "Fix this." Stage 2: eight-agent orchestration, 18 slash commands, custom workflows. You feel like a genius. Stage 3: back to short prompts. Elite looks like beginner. Most people are stuck in stage 2. Which stage are you in? Be honest. 𝟱/ 𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗠𝗣𝗧𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗧𝗢𝗢 𝗟𝗢𝗡𝗚? 𝗬𝗢𝗨𝗥 𝗔𝗥𝗖𝗛𝗜𝗧𝗘𝗖𝗧𝗨𝗥𝗘 𝗜𝗦 𝗪𝗥𝗢𝗡𝗚. I tested this. 4 out of 5 times the agent was forcing a feature my structure made hard. The fix wasn't a better prompt. It was a refactor. 𝟲/ 𝗖𝗟𝗜 𝗢𝗩𝗘𝗥 𝗠𝗖𝗣𝘀. Every MCP injects its full schema into every prompt. Silent token tax. I found 81 tool definitions loading on every message. 𝟳/ 𝗦𝗛𝗢𝗥𝗧𝗘𝗥 𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗠𝗣𝗧𝗦, 𝗠𝗢𝗥𝗘 𝗦𝗖𝗥𝗘𝗘𝗡𝗦𝗛𝗢𝗧𝗦. 50% of prompts should be screenshots. The rest? 1-2 sentences. Writing paragraphs? Still stage 2. 𝟴/ 𝗗𝗢𝗡'𝗧 𝗦𝗣𝗘𝗖, 𝗗𝗜𝗦𝗖𝗨𝗦𝗦. Feed the model websites, screenshots, references. Ask "give me 3 options" before building anything. 𝟵/ 𝗔𝗚𝗘𝗡𝗧𝗦 𝗪𝗢𝗥𝗞 𝗕𝗘𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥 𝗢𝗡 𝗕𝗢𝗥𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗧𝗘𝗖𝗛. Stable APIs, more training data. Switching from niche libraries to standard ones cut my agent errors in half. 𝟭𝟬/ 𝗥𝗘𝗙𝗔𝗖𝗧𝗢𝗥𝗦 𝗔𝗥𝗘 𝗖𝗛𝗘𝗔𝗣. 𝗗𝗢 𝗜𝗧 𝗢𝗙𝗧𝗘𝗡. Sonnet handles in 3 minutes what took me half a day. 20% of time should go to refactoring. jscpd, knip, ESLint. Agents clean their own mess on a schedule. 𝟭𝟭/ 𝟯𝟬𝟬𝗞 𝗟𝗜𝗡𝗘𝗦. 𝗢𝗡𝗘 𝗗𝗘𝗩. 𝟭𝟬𝟬% 𝗔𝗚𝗘𝗡𝗧-𝗪𝗥𝗜𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗡. Steinberger: "I ship code I never read" 𝟭𝟮/ 𝗧𝗘𝗦𝗧 𝗪𝗛𝗘𝗡 𝗖𝗢𝗡𝗧𝗘𝗫𝗧 𝗜𝗦 𝗙𝗥𝗘𝗦𝗛. Build, test, move on. Wait a day and the agent starts from zero. 𝟭𝟯/ 𝗣𝗥 𝗥𝗘𝗩𝗜𝗘𝗪: 𝗜𝗡𝗧𝗘𝗡𝗧 𝗙𝗜𝗥𝗦𝗧. First question: "Do you understand the intent of this PR?" Then point it to code it hasn't seen. Watch it connect dots. 𝟭𝟰/ "𝗩𝗜𝗕𝗘 𝗖𝗢𝗗𝗜𝗡𝗚" 𝗜𝗦 𝗔 𝗦𝗟𝗨𝗥. Tried it once, blamed the tool. Same as playing piano once and saying the instrument is broken. ⸻ Which number changed how you think? Drop it below. ♻️ Repost if someone in your network is in Stage 2 right now.

posts.content: Paul Iusztin View Paul Iusztin’s profile • 2nd Senior AI Engineer • Founder @ Decoding AI • Author @ LLM Engineer’s Handbook ~ I ship AI products and teach you about the process. 1mo • 1mo Visible to everyone I’ve spent the past 2+ years building and breaking AI agents in production. Here’s an uncomfortable truth: Most agents fail because of subtle system design mistakes. And there are 6 of them to be precise: 1. Treating the context window as an afterthought 2. Starting with complicated solutions 3. Building agents when a workflow will do 4. Fragile parsing of LLM outputs 5. Forgetting agents need planning 6. Not starting with AI evals from day zero Individually, they look small. In production, they compound into disasters pretty fast. After seeing these patterns repeat again and again, I wrote them down. And turned them into a free 6-day email course. Each day covers one mistake we’ve seen break real systems. You’ll learn: • When you don’t need an agent • Why naive ReAct loops are brittle • How to think about context intentionally • Why planning is not optional • Why evals are your north star from day zero If you’re building agents in 2026, you'll need architectural judgment. This guide is my attempt to compress 2+ years of painful lessons into 6 emails. It’s completely free. ------ UPDATE: The response to this post has been far greater than I expected. I'm still tending to all the responses manually, but it will take some time to get through them. posts.title: Patrick SZYMKOWIAK View Patrick SZYMKOWIAK’s profile • 3rd+ Founder / builder / RTK / Kexa 1mo • 1mo Visible to everyone
posts.content: Patrick SZYMKOWIAK View Patrick SZYMKOWIAK’s profile • 3rd+ Founder / builder / RTK / Kexa 1mo • 1mo Visible to everyone Début 2026, je brûlais mon forfait Claude Code en quelques heures. Pas à cause de prompts complexes. Juste du développement normal. Chaque commande que mon agent IA exécutait — git log, cargo test, ls -la — injectait des milliers de tokens inutiles dans la fenêtre de contexte. Des barres de progression. Des tests qui passent. Du formatage verbeux. Du bruit pur. Alors j'ai construit RTK — Rust Token Killer. En le développant, j'ai réalisé l'ampleur du problème : environ 80% des tokens consommés étaient du bruit. Un proxy CLI en Rust qui compresse les sorties de commandes AVANT qu'elles n'atteignent le contexte de l'agent IA. Mes vrais chiffres après 15 jours : → 7 061 commandes → 29.3M tokens en entrée → 4.8M en sortie → 24.6M tokens économisés (83.7%) Concrètement : - cargo test : 155 lignes → 3 lignes (98%) - git status : 119 caractères → 28 caractères - Sessions sensiblement plus longues - Les rate limits ? Beaucoup moins fréquents. Un seul binaire Rust. Zéro dépendance. Installation en une commande. Aujourd'hui, en 3 semaines, RTK c'est 521 ⭐ sur GitHub, 46 forks, ~1 000 utilisateurs actifs, et une compatibilité avec Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Aider, Codex, Windsurf et Cline. Si vous développez avec un agent IA et que vous sentez que ça rame ou que ça coupe, il y a de fortes chances que votre contexte soit saturé de bruit. Vous utilisez déjà RTK ? Gemini Live processes what it sees and hears over WebSocket, decides if action is needed, routes tool calls through OpenClaw, and speaks the result back. No Meta glasses? No problem. posts.title: A Practical Guide to Modern Document Understanding
posts.content: Markus Kuehnle View Markus Kuehnle’s profile • 2nd ML/AI Engineer | Building End-to-End Systems | Helping engineers ship AI from scratch to production 8mo • 8mo Visible to everyone Tesseract can’t answer: “What are the top 3 risks in this contract?” That’s where vision-language models take over. OCR still works.. but when context matters, it’s not enough. Let’s walk through the shift: 📌 𝟭. 𝗖𝗹𝗮𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗰 𝗢𝗖𝗥 𝗽𝗶𝗽𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗹𝗶𝗺𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗱. You extract text → try to rebuild structure → hope it holds. But real documents aren’t clean: • Tables inside tables • Fonts and spacing that carry meaning • Layouts that don’t follow any order OCR is great for overlays, forms, and precise spans. It struggles when you need deeper understanding. 📌 𝟮. 𝗣𝗮𝗟𝗜 𝘀𝗸𝗶𝗽𝘀 𝘁𝗲𝘅𝘁 𝗲𝘅𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗿𝗲𝗹𝘆. PaLI is trained across 100+ languages. You give it a document image → it answers your question. “What’s the invoice total?” → “$1,294.55” It combines: • ViT (Vision Transformer) to encode the image • mT5 (Multilingual Text-to-Text Transformer) to generate the answer No text layer. No bounding boxes. Just reasoning over pixels. 📌 𝟯. 𝗖𝗼𝗹𝗣𝗮𝗟𝗜 𝗴𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝗳𝘂𝗿𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿: 𝗥𝗲𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘃𝗮𝗹 + 𝗩𝗤𝗔 ColPaLI = PaLI-Gemma + ColBERT-style retriever It: → Splits PDFs into visual pages → Encodes each page with token-wise embeddings → Retrieves relevant ones with late interaction → Answers based on the best-matching context Good for search + QA over large sets of scanned PDFs. 🧠 Bookmark this section if you're designing a doc understanding pipeline. 📌 𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝘁𝗼 𝘂𝘀𝗲 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁? 𝗨𝘀𝗲 𝗢𝗖𝗥 𝗶𝗳: → You need precise fields, coordinates, or overlays → You’re doing form parsing or tabular extraction → You want full control, fast execution 𝗨𝘀𝗲 𝗣𝗮𝗟𝗜 𝗶𝗳: → You want end-to-end answers from document images → You deal with multilingual or unstructured scans → Layout context matters more than exact positions 𝗨𝘀𝗲 𝗖𝗼𝗹𝗣𝗮𝗟𝗜 𝗶𝗳: → You’re working with many PDFs, not just one → You need retrieval + VQA → You’re building document copilots or visual RAG systems The goal isn’t to replace OCR. It’s to know when OCR is not enough. PaLI and ColPaLI bring in context, layout, and reasoning and open up new ways to work with documents that don’t follow rules. 💬 𝗙𝘂𝗹𝗹 𝗖𝗼𝗹𝗣𝗮𝗟𝗜 𝘄𝗮𝗹𝗸𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 ↓ Curious what you’d build with it. ♻️ Repost to help someone in your network. A Practical Guide to Modern Document Understanding

posts.content: Avi Chawla View Avi Chawla’s profile • 3rd+ Co-founder DailyDoseofDS | IIT Varanasi | ex-AI Engineer MastercardAI | Newsletter (150k+) 1mo • 1mo Visible to everyone Finally, devs can vibe code all the way to production! There's a frustrating pattern that every developer using AI coding agents has experienced. The Agent builds a beautiful frontend in mins. It sets up working API routes and lays out the component architecture. But then it hits a wall the moment backend configuration is needed. For instance, to enable auth, devs need to manually create Firebase projects, click through auth tabs, enable OAuth providers one by one, and copy credentials between dashboards. That's 15+ manual steps, and Agents can't do any of them because every backend platform today was designed for human devs navigating dashboards, not for Agents invoking APIs. And when Agents try to interact with Firebase or Supabase through MCP servers, they get fragmented info like table names without schema details or security configurations. So Agents end up guessing, hallucinating, and generating broken code that devs have to fix manually. But this is actually a solvable problem. The backend can be designed from the ground up for AI Agents with complete context in single calls, zero-config defaults, and machine-readable errors. This exact approach is now available in InsForge, a recently-trending fully open-source backend specifically built for AI coding Agents. Here's what InsForge enables: - Agents see the full database picture in one call, so they stop guessing - Auth with Google, GitHub, and more, without any dashboard setup - Storage and AI features that Agents can set up themselves. Performance-wise, InsForge: - is almost 2x more accurate than Supabase MCP - leads to 1.6x faster execution - uses 30% fewer tokens The video below shows InsForge in action. It's a ChatGPT clone I built entirely with Claude Code using InsForge as the backend. It has auth, database, storage, and AI integration, and building it required zero manual configuration. InsForge works with any AI coding agent, including Cursor, Claude Code, Windsurf, and Codex. You can use all the primitives together or just pick what you need, like database only or auth only. The repo is fully open-source under Apache 2.0, so you can see the full implementation and try it yourself. I have shared the GitHub repo in the comments! ____ Find me → Avi Chawla Every day, I share tutorials and insights on DS, ML, LLMs, and RAGs.

posts.content: Paolo Perrone View Paolo Perrone’s profile • 2nd No BS AI/ML Content | ML Engineer with a Plot Twist 🥷100M+ Views 📝 1mo • 1mo Visible to everyone They told you 70B models need 80GB VRAM. They lied. AirLLM runs Llama 70B on a 4GB GPU. No quantization. No distillation. No pruning. The trick: layer-wise inference. Instead of loading the entire model into VRAM, it loads one layer at a time from disk. Your GPU only ever holds one layer. The rest lives on disk. What you can run: → Llama 70B on 4GB VRAM → Llama 405B on 8GB VRAM → Qwen2.5, Mixtral, ChatGLM all supported pip install airllm from airllm import AutoModel model = AutoModel.from_pretrained("garage-bAInd/Platypus2-70B-instruct") input_tokens = model.tokenizer(input_text, return_tensors="pt", truncation=True, max_length=128) output = model.generate( input_tokens['input_ids'].cuda(), max_new_tokens=20) Standard transformers API. That's it. Optional: 4-bit compression for 3x speed boost. model = AutoModel.from_pretrained("...", compression='4bit') Trade-off: slower inference than full VRAM loading. But if you don't have the VRAM, you don't have options. Works on MacOS with Apple Silicon too. 1.9k GitHub stars. Apache 2.0. → github.com/lyogavin/airllm 💾 Save for when your GPU budget doesn't match your model ambitions ♻️ Repost if you've ever closed a tab because "requires 80GB VRAM"

posts.title: Electric Vehicle Charging Decision using Dynamic Programming medium.com
posts.content: Tejas G. Tejas G. View Tejas G.’s profile • 2nd Lead OR consultant @ Fico| Operations research And Data Science | Logistics | Price Optimization 2mo • 2mo Visible to everyone Building on the previous discussions on Dynamic Programming (DP), this article puts the framework to work on a concrete, end-to-end optimization problem: Electric Vehicle Charging Decisions. Going beyond the conceptual level, the focus here is on how to actually model and solve a realistic sequential decision problem. EV charging naturally fits the DP framework because energy levels evolve over time, charging decisions are interdependent, and the objective is to balance cost and feasibility across a planning horizon. This write-up demonstrates: - Formulating the EV charging problem as a multi-stage DP - Clear definitions of states, actions, transitions, and costs - Step-by-step construction of the Bellman recursion - A complete Python implementation, walking through each DP step from initialization to policy extraction The goal isn’t just to solve an EV problem, but to show how DP thinking translates from theory to a practical OR model, step by step. If you’re curious how Dynamic Programming moves from abstract principles to a tangible optimization workflow, this article bridges that gap. Electric Vehicle Charging Decision using Dynamic Programming medium.com

posts.title: Aurimas Griciūnas View Aurimas Griciūnas’ profile • 2nd Founder @ SwirlAI • Ex-CPO @ neptune.ai (Acquired by OpenAI) • U
posts.content: Aurimas Griciūnas View Aurimas Griciūnas’ profile • 2nd Founder @ SwirlAI • Ex-CPO @ neptune.ai (Acquired by OpenAI) • UpSkilling the Next Generation of AI Talent • Author of SwirlAI Newsletter • Public Speaker 2mo • 2mo Visible to everyone 𝗧𝗼𝗼𝗹 𝗖𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘃𝗶𝗮 𝗠𝗖𝗣 vs. implementing it 𝗡𝗮𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁. What's the difference? Recently there have been many MCP vs. Function Calling articles floating around. Let’s simplify. ❗️ 𝗖𝗹𝗮𝗿𝗶𝗳𝘆𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗱𝗲𝘁𝗮𝗶𝗹: Function Calling and Tool Use in Agentic Systems are almost the same thing. You can implement tools via functions, the only difference is that functions are usually used to enforce stricter structure to the input and output schema. 𝘜𝘴𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘔𝘊𝘗 𝘵𝘰 𝘦𝘹𝘱𝘰𝘴𝘦 𝘵𝘰𝘰𝘭𝘴 𝘵𝘰 𝘺𝘰𝘶𝘳 𝘈𝘨𝘦𝘯𝘵𝘴: ℹ️ In this case your Agent becomes an MCP Host and implements one or more MCP Clients to communicate with MCP Servers. 𝟭. User Query is passed to the Agent (usually a Python application). 𝟮. The application implements MCP Client and via it retrieves all available tools from the MCP servers. 𝟯. The list of available Tools is passed together with the User Query to a LLM via a prompt. The LLM figures out which tools need to be invoked and with what parameters. 𝟰. The Agent application communicates with the MCP server (via MCP Client) again and sends the tool execution request. After execution completes the Agent receives the required data. 𝟱. User Query is sent to the LLM together with the data retrieved by the Tool calls. 𝟲. The answer is constructed and returned to the user via the Agent. 𝘜𝘴𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘕𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘷𝘦 𝘍𝘶𝘯𝘤𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘊𝘢𝘭𝘭𝘪𝘯𝘨: 𝟭. User Query is passed to the Agent (usually a Python application). 𝟮. All of the available Functions/Tools are defined as part of the Agent code (procedural memory). 𝟯. The list of available Tools is passed together with the User Query to a LLM via a prompt. The LLM figures out which functions need to be invoked and with what parameters. 𝟰. The Agent application directly executes the functions. 𝟱. User Query is sent to the LLM together with the data retrieved after function execution. 𝟲. The answer is constructed and returned to the user via the Agent. Learn to build both architectures hands-on in my End-to-End AI Engineering Bootcamp: https://lnkd.in/dagWE5r3 . We are kicking off today, last chance to register until the end of tomorrow. 🎁 Use code LASTCHANCE at checkout for 10% off. 𝗠𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵𝘁𝘀: ❗️ Will MCP eat up the practice of Native Function Calling? If we adopt the standard then I believe so. ❗️ Will MCP compete with LLM Orchestration frameworks? I believe MCP will replace the Tool use abstractions as they are used today and frameworks will be responsible mostly for managing the topology and state of the Agentic systems long term. Are you using MCP already to expose Tools to your Agents? Let me know in the comments. 👇

But that knowledge doesn’t stick until you’ve applied it. Here’s how to practice correctly: • Choose a problem that sparks your curiosity, then use it to scope and design your central project. • Start deterministically first. Build explicit workflows where every step is debuggable and predictable. • Introduce agents where ambiguity exists • Watch where the agentic loops add latency, cost, or unpredictability to learn the failure modes. • Explore orchestration by combining multiple tools, APIs, and most importantly, multiple agents into a single flow. In our AI Agents course, we use a Research Agent and a Writing Workflow as concrete case studies. But the same patterns apply no matter what project you pick. posts.content: Michel Antônio Gonçalves View Michel Antônio Gonçalves’ profile • 3rd+ Data Developer at CI&T 3mo • 3mo Visible to everyone In BigQuery, LIMIT limits your results, but not your bill It felt bizarre: I would add LIMIT 1000, LIMIT 100, or even LIMIT 10 in BigQuery, yet the query would still scan over 100GB. For newcomers, especially those tasked with validating data directly in production, this is a terrifying rite of passage. Unlike traditional row-based databases like Postgres or MySQL, LIMIT in BigQuery does not reduce the volume of data scanned from disk. It scans the entire column first and only then discards the extra rows to give you your 10 lines. It's like paying for the full buffet, but only getting to eat a fraction of the salad. This is where TABLESAMPLE becomes a life-saver and, literally, a money-saver. Unlike LIMIT, using TABLESAMPLE SYSTEM (1 PERCENT) instructs the execution engine to scan only a random sample of data blocks. If your table is 1tb: With LIMIT 10 / 100 / 1000: You could still process the full 1tb. With TABLESAMPLE (1%): You only process around 10gb. The bottom line is: if you just need to check the "shape" of the data or test a logic, stop relying on LIMIT and start using TABLESAMPLE. The budget will thank you! #BigQuery #DataEngineering #GoogleCloud #DataAnalytics #SQLTips #CloudOptimization

posts.content: Paul Iusztin View Paul Iusztin’s profile • 2nd Senior AI Engineer • Founder @ Decoding AI • Author @ LLM Engineer’s Handbook ~ I ship AI products and teach you about the process. 3mo • 3mo Visible to everyone I've read a lot of books this year... But this one stands out as one of the most useful reads for AI engineers: → LLMOps: Managing Large Language Models in Production by Abi Aryan ☯︎ The title undersells it. This isn’t “just” an LLMOps book... It’s one of the clearest end-to-end guides for anyone trying to ship LLM applications. A few highlights that stood out: 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗘𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗟𝗟𝗠 This chapter alone could be an entire book. It walks through the real foundations behind every production system: • Collecting and cleaning datasets • Keeping data fresh (a massively underestimated problem) • Structured vs vector storage • Versioning, lineage, and synthetic data A lot of AI engineers underestimate how much their product relies on data engineering. This section makes that clear. 𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹 𝗔𝗱𝗮𝗽𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗥𝗲𝗮𝗹 𝗦𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺𝘀 Fine-tuning, ensembling, and applying your data to real workloads. Even though they don’t call it out explicitly, this is where RAG should live as a way to adapt models without touching weights. 𝗗𝗲𝗽𝗹𝗼𝘆𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗦𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗬ou get practical guidance on: • Serving models efficiently • KV caching, embedding caching, and latency tradeoffs • How to expose LLMs as APIs properly • Autoscaling and cost optimisation This is the stuff engineers usually learn the hard way. 𝗘𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗠𝗼𝗻𝗶𝘁𝗼𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 The book’s final section should honestly be half the book. It breaks down: • RAG-specific metrics • Agentic evaluation • Drift detection • When to trigger retraining/rebuilding • Why traditional metrics do not work for LLMs If you’re deploying anything beyond a toy system, this chapter is gold. 𝗚𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗦𝗲𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆 Prompt injection, jailbreaks, audits, privacy, compliance. It’s unglamorous, but this is what production actually looks like. 𝗖𝗹𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴, 𝗣𝗮𝗿𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗹𝗶𝘀𝗺, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗛𝗮𝗿𝗱𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗦𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴 Data parallelism, model parallelism, pipeline parallelism, DeepSpeed, ZeRO, kernel fusion, precision scaling… Even as an AI engineer, this section helped me connect missing dots. 𝗛𝗲𝗿𝗲'𝘀 𝗺𝘆 𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗲𝗮𝘄𝗮𝘆: If you're getting into AI engineering, especially the ops or infrastructure side, this is one of the best primers you can read. If you're more experienced, you won’t need to read it end-to-end. posts.title: Shirin Khosravi Jam View Shirin Khosravi Jam’s profile • 2nd Sr. Data Scientist/ AI Engineer | Data Science, RAG, AI Age
posts.content: Shirin Khosravi Jam View Shirin Khosravi Jam’s profile • 2nd Sr. Data Scientist/ AI Engineer | Data Science, RAG, AI Agents, & MLOps | Germany’s Top Female Voice in AI (Favikon) 🇩🇪 | 235k+ AI/ML Community 🤯 | Opinions are my own! 4mo • 4mo Visible to everyone 69.99% of AI Engineers don't know how to structure a repo This is how you can structure your GenAI repo 👇 Here’s how we structure production-grade FastAPI based GenAI systems: 🔹 𝘀𝗿𝗰/ - 𝗖𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗔𝗽𝗽𝗹𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗟𝗼𝗴𝗶𝗰 We use a layered + domain-first architecture - the same structure that powers robust ML/AI systems in production. Let’s break it down: 1️⃣ 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹𝘀/ → SQLAlchemy ORM models ↳ Defines your database schema: tables, types, indexes ↳ E.g. academic paper metadata: title, authors, abstract 2️⃣ 𝘀𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗺𝗮𝘀/ → Pydantic models for data validation ↳ Type-safe request/response structures ↳ Handles optional fields, default values, constraints 3️⃣ 𝗿𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀/ → FastAPI route definitions ↳ Logical grouping of endpoints (e.g., /search, /upload) ↳ Auto-generates clean Swagger/OpenAPI docs ✅ Exposes your system cleanly to devs, tools, and UIs. 4️⃣ 𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗼𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗼𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘀/ → DB interaction layer ↳ Clean abstraction over SQL queries ↳ Makes business logic readable + testable ✅ No raw SQL scattered in your app. Easy to test and evolve. 5️⃣ 𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗶𝗰𝗲𝘀/ - The brain of your application → Logic organized by domain, not just CRUD e.g.: ↳ opensearch/ → Hybrid retrieval logic ✅ Modular by design: swap, extend, or evolve features without chaos. 6️⃣ 𝗱𝗯/ → Database engine config ↳ Connection pooling, retry logic, async sessions ✅ Rock-solid DB handling. No “random connection errors” in prod. 7️⃣ 𝗺𝗮𝗶𝗻.𝗽𝘆 → FastAPI entry point ↳ Imports routes, applies middlewares, sets up CORS + logging ✅ Single source of truth for app startup. 8️⃣ 𝗺𝗶𝗱𝗱𝗹𝗲𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗲𝘀.𝗽𝘆 / 𝗲𝘅𝗰𝗲𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀.𝗽𝘆 → Reliability and observability layer ↳ Logs tracebacks ↳ Converts random errors into structured API messages ✅ Debugging and monitoring become predictable. 🔹 𝗕𝗲𝘆𝗼𝗻𝗱 𝘀𝗿𝗰/: 𝗜𝗻𝗳𝗿𝗮 + 𝗧𝗼𝗼𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴 1️⃣ 𝗗𝗼𝗰𝗸𝗲𝗿𝗳𝗶𝗹𝗲 + 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗼𝘀𝗲.𝘆𝗺𝗹 → One-line infra bootstrapping: ↳ Starts: FastAPI, PostgreSQL, OpenSearch, Airflow, Ollama ✅ Works on every machine. No setup nightmares. 2️⃣ 𝗠𝗮𝗸𝗲𝗳𝗶𝗹𝗲 → Simplifies commands like: ↳ make test, make lint, make up, etc. ✅ Standardized developer workflows. 3️⃣ 𝗽𝗿𝗲-𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗶𝘁-𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗳𝗶𝗴 . 𝘆𝗮𝗺𝗹 → Linting + formatting (Ruff, Black, isort) → Prevents bad code from being committed ✅ Clean code. Enforced automatically. 4️⃣ 𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁𝘀/ → Pytest structure ↳ Unit tests with fixtures and mocks ✅ You can confidently refactor without breaking things. 5️⃣ 𝗻𝗼𝘁𝗲𝗯𝗼𝗼𝗸𝘀/ → Analysis or test notebooks PS: As you put the repo into production there would more components added, e.g. CI/CD, infrastructure, etc. Want to see it in action? Check our Zero to RAG series: → Blog: https://lnkd.in/dHpeuizv → Code: https://lnkd.in/dCYbsY3c ♻️ Repost to help other engineers 💚 ➕ Join 32.500+ serious AI/ML builders here: https://lnkd.in/ds_SzEUH

posts.title: Brij kishore Pandey View Brij kishore Pandey’s profile • 2nd AI Architect & Engineer | AI Strategist 4mo • 4mo Visible t
posts.content: Brij kishore Pandey View Brij kishore Pandey’s profile • 2nd AI Architect & Engineer | AI Strategist 4mo • 4mo Visible to everyone Most Generative AI projects don’t fail because of weak models — they fail because the engineering foundation is weak. Teams often begin with prompts, APIs, and notebooks. But when it’s time to scale, integrate, audit, or productionize, everything starts to break. What really decides if your AI project moves from demo to product? How well it is structured from day one. The visual you see is a structured Generative AI project layout. It covers modularity, maintainability, configuration management, prompt engineering, token usage, and logging. It helps solve common challenges like: • Unstructured notebooks and prototype chaos • Hardcoded prompts and model settings • No token tracking, caching, or rate limiting • Mixing prompt logic with core application code • Difficulty moving from proof-of-concept to production What this structure includes effectively: • YAML-based configurations for prompts, models, and logging • Modular LLM clients (GPT, Claude, Base) • Prompt engineering utilities: templates, chaining, few-shot design • Token counting, caching, logging, and rate limiters • Separate example scripts and experimental notebooks • Clear separation between utilities, handlers, and core logic What is not included — but should be added in any production-ready GenAI system: Security and Governance • Secret management (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) • PII handling and compliance safeguards • Guardrails, content moderation, responsible use Observability and Monitoring • Token usage analytics and latency tracking • Failure metrics, tool-call history, retry insights • Integration with LangSmith, Honeycomb, or Arize Testing and Evaluation • Prompt regression testing • Response quality evaluation frameworks (RAGAS, TruLens) • Model behaviour tracking across iterations Agent, Memory, and Context Management • Memory layers (short-term, long-term, vector-based) • Agent orchestration with structured task flows • Document retrieval, tool routing, function handlers Ops and Deployment • CI/CD and container orchestration • Scalable API deployment (FastAPI, Lambda, Kubernetes) • API gateway, authentication, throttling, access control This framework is a great start. But scaling GenAI is less about prompts—and more about disciplined engineering. Structure is not just documentation. In AI systems, structure itself is a feature. The complete GitHub template code for this structure is available in the comments.

posts.title: Abi Aryan ☯︎ View Abi Aryan ☯︎’s profile • 2nd ML Research Engineer | Author: LLMOps & GPU Engineering | Making AI Syste
posts.content: Abi Aryan ☯︎ View Abi Aryan ☯︎’s profile • 2nd ML Research Engineer | Author: LLMOps & GPU Engineering | Making AI Systems go brrrr... 4mo • 4mo Visible to everyone So many people keep asking me this ⁣“𝘢𝘣𝘪, 𝘸𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘨𝘱𝘶 𝘴𝘩𝘰𝘶𝘭𝘥 𝘐 𝘨𝘦𝘵 𝘧𝘰𝘳 𝘮𝘺 𝘱𝘦𝘳𝘴𝘰𝘯𝘢𝘭 AI 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘫𝘦𝘤𝘵𝘴 𝘢𝘵 𝘩𝘰𝘮𝘦” so i just dumped everything in one table.. No affiliate links, no one sponsored this (hi NVIDIA hi AMD hi Intel Corporation 😂 👋). I can assure you I still have a lot of a little bit of soul left in me 😝 ⁣𝖶𝖾𝗅𝗅, 𝖺𝖼𝗍𝗎𝖺𝗅𝗅𝗒 𝗂𝗍'𝗌 𝖺 𝖽𝗋𝖺𝖿𝗍 𝖿𝗋𝗈𝗆 𝗍𝗁𝖾 𝖠𝗉𝗉𝖾𝗇𝖽𝗂𝗑 𝗈𝖿 𝗆𝗒 𝖦𝖯𝖴 𝖤𝗇𝗀𝗂𝗇𝖾𝖾𝗋𝗂𝗇𝗀 𝖻𝗈𝗈𝗄 𝗍𝗁𝖺𝗍 𝖨 𝖺𝗆 𝖼𝗎𝗋𝗋𝖾𝗇𝗍𝗅𝗒 𝗐𝗋𝗂𝗍𝗂𝗇𝗀..⁣ So key Takeaways on GPU Performance for LLMs: - 𝟒𝟎𝟗𝟎⁣⁣ is still my preferred starter. - 𝐑𝐓𝐗 𝐀𝟔𝟎𝟎𝟎 (𝟒𝟖 𝐆𝐁 𝐄𝐂𝐂, 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟐): It can handle very large models like 130B (Q5) or 405B (Q3) on a single card, assuming optimized frameworks and reasonable batch sizes. Still viable for daily use. - 𝐑𝐓𝐗 𝟓𝟎𝟗𝟎: Extremely fast, achieving ~120–140 tokens/sec on 70B Q6, but 32 GB VRAM can be limiting for models that previously ran on 48 GB. High speed, lower memory capacity trade-off. Do not recommend. - 𝐑𝐗 𝟕𝟗𝟎𝟎 𝐗𝐓𝐗: Offers VRAM comparable to a 4090 at a lower cost. ROCm software support has improved significantly, making it a more practical AMD option for LLMs, though CUDA remains more optimized. - 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐥 𝐀𝐫𝐜 𝐁𝟓𝟖𝟎: Surprisingly capable for medium-sized models like 70B Q4. A cost-effective option for those on a budget, though driver maturity and ecosystem support are still developing. - 𝐇𝐚𝐢𝐥𝐨-𝟖𝐋: Ultra low-power option for smaller models (~7B). Achieves 35–40 tokens/sec at ~4 watts, ideal for always-on, energy-efficient deployment. I still suggest AMD mostly for racks and SLMs, 𝐈'𝐥𝐥 𝐝𝐫𝐨𝐩 𝐦𝐲 𝐚𝐧𝐚𝐥𝐲𝐬𝐢𝐬 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐩𝐫𝐢𝐬𝐞𝐬 𝐧𝐞𝐱𝐭. Treat this as your rough guide, hope it helps someone. Enjoy!

posts.content: Akshay Pachaar View Akshay Pachaar’s profile • 3rd+ Co-Founder DailyDoseOfDS | BITS Pilani | 3 Patents | X (187K+) 4mo • 4mo Visible to everyone Meta just changed real-time object detection forever. Their latest model SAM 3 is a beast: Before SAM 3: collect data, train custom object detector, use tracker to estimate object motion - days After SAM 3: track anything with text prompt - seconds Let's understand why it's a big deal: Companies spend millions paying humans to label images and videos frame by frame. A single autonomous driving dataset? Months of work, hundreds of annotators, millions in cost. Without labeled data, you can't train custom models. Without custom models, you're stuck with generic solutions. This is why most companies never move past pilots. SAM 3 breaks this cycle. First let's look at the evolution: SAM 1 segmented objects when you clicked on them. Revolutionary, but one object at a time. SAM 2 added video tracking with memory. Game-changing, but you still manually prompted every object. SAM 3 changes everything with text prompts. Type "yellow school bus" and it finds ALL of them in your image or video. Not just one. Every instance across thousands of frames. Now here's where people get confused: "Can't I just use GPT-5 or Gemini for this?" No, and here's why that's a terrible approach. Large multimodal LLMs are great for reasoning, but they're slow and expensive for production visual tasks. You're paying API costs per image, waiting seconds for responses, getting inconsistent results. SAM 3 runs in 30 milliseconds on a single GPU for 100+ objects. That's 100x faster, and you own the infrastructure. More importantly, SAM 3 gives you precise pixel-level masks, not descriptions. Try asking an LLM to segment every defective part on a manufacturing line in real-time. It won't work. SAM 3 does this effortlessly. The real breakthrough is their data engine. SAM 3 is trained on 4 million unique visual concepts. It handles everything: - Text-based concept search - Interactive refinement with clicks - Video tracking across frames - Zero-shot detection of new concepts The model is open source. Weights, code, and benchmarks are on GitHub. If you're building computer vision applications, this is the foundation model to evaluate. The annotation time savings alone will pay for integration costs within weeks. posts.title: Pallavi Ahuja View Pallavi Ahuja’s profile • 2nd AI | Software Engineering | Writes @techNmak 4mo • 4mo Visible to every
posts.content: Pallavi Ahuja View Pallavi Ahuja’s profile • 2nd AI | Software Engineering | Writes @techNmak 4mo • 4mo Visible to everyone Sebastian Raschka, PhD continues to be one of the most vital educators in the AI community. His breakdown of the 2025 LLM landscape is a massive service to the field. He brilliantly connects the dots on a trend many have felt but haven't articulated. If you haven't read his blog yet, I highly recommend it. In the meantime, here is the architectural cheat sheet of the 17 models he analyzed: ➡️ DeepSeek V3 & R1 → MLA (Multi-Head Latent Attention). → Compresses Key-Value tensors to slash memory. Uses a "Shared Expert" + → 8 routed experts. ➡️ DeepSeek V3.2 → Sparse Attention. → A linear attention variant trading some modeling accuracy for massive computational speedups. ➡️ Llama 4 → Classic MoE. → Uses fewer but larger experts than DeepSeek. Stiff-arms MLA to stick with standard GQA. ➡️ Qwen3 (Dense & MoE) → Simplified MoE. → Dropped the "Shared Expert" design entirely to simplify inference logic. ➡️ Qwen3-Next → Gated DeltaNet. → A speed demon using Multi-Token Prediction (predicts future tokens in parallel) + Linear Attention hybrid. ➡️ Kimi K2 & Thinking → Muon Optimizer. → A 1-Trillion parameter giant. The "Thinking" variant extends context to 256k. ➡️ Kimi Linear → Linear Hybrid. → A 3:1 ratio of Gated DeltaNet (Linear) to MLA (Full Attention). Matches full attention performance with linear efficiency. ➡️ Gemma 3 → Sliding Window Attention. → Uses a 5:1 ratio—5 layers of local (windowed) attention for every 1 layer of global attention. ➡️ Gemma 3n → Per-Layer Embeddings. → Optimized for mobile. It streams parameters from CPU/SSD storage on demand. ➡️ OLMo 2 → Stability First. → Uses Post-Norm (RMSNorm after blocks) and QK-Norm to prevent training loss spikes. ➡️ Mistral Small 3.1 → Pure GQA. → Abandoned sliding window attention. Optimized for raw latency and throughput. ➡️ SmolLM3 → NoPE (No Positional Embeddings). → Removes RoPE entirely. Relies purely on the causal mask for token order. ➡️ GPT-OSS (OpenAI) → Bias Units & Sinks. → A wider architecture that curiously brings back Bias terms and uses learned "Attention Sinks" for stability. ➡️ Grok 2.5 → SwiGLU Shared Expert. → Validates DeepSeek’s approach by using a massive SwiGLU module as an always-on shared expert. ➡️ GLM-4.5 → Dense-to-Sparse. → Keeps the first 3 layers dense before switching to MoE to stabilize early feature extraction. ➡️ MiniMax-M1 → Lightning Attention. → An early linear attention variant focused purely on efficiency. ➡️ MiniMax-M2 → Per-Layer QK-Norm. → Uses a unique norm for each attention head + Partial RoPE (rotates only half the dimensions). We are seeing the 'Cambrian Explosion' of the Transformer. → Cache: DeepSeek (MLA) → Window: Gemma (Sliding) → Speed: Qwen/Kimi (Linear Attention) (I’ll put the blog link in the comments.) ♻️ Repost to save someone $$$ and a lot of confusion. ✔️ You can follow Pallavi, for more insights.

posts.content: Paolo Perrone View Paolo Perrone’s profile • 2nd No BS AI/ML Content | ML Engineer with a Plot Twist 🥷100M+ Views 📝 4mo • 4mo Visible to everyone Sebastian Raschka, PhD just exposed the biggest secret in AI. After dissecting 9 flagship LLMs, he found something nobody wants to admit: We haven't invented a new architecture in 7 years. The evidence is damning: • DeepSeek V3: 671B parameters, still a transformer • Kimi K2: 1 TRILLION parameters, still a transformer • GPT-OSS: OpenAI's latest, still a transformer • Llama 4: Meta's flagship, still a transformer Every "breakthrough" model? Same skeleton. Different makeup. Here's what's actually happening: DeepSeek V3/R1: Compressed attention (MLA) + expert routing (MoE) Gemma 3: Sliding windows to fake longer context SmolLM3: Removed position embeddings entirely (!) Kimi K2: Just made DeepSeek bigger The brutal reality: • No new architectures since "Attention is All You Need" (2017) • Every innovation = efficiency hack • We're polishing, not inventing 671 billion parameters. 1 trillion parameters. Same. Damn. Architecture. While everyone's chasing parameter counts, Sebastian mapped the actual mutations: • MoE: Use 37B of your 671B parameters • Sliding attention: Pretend you have infinite context • MLA: Compress your KV cache and pray This isn't innovation. It's optimization theater. The most honest technical analysis you'll read this year. Read it. Then ask yourself: If we can't innovate past transformers, what happens when we hit the parameter wall? ♻️ Repost if you appreciate actual technical depth over hype

But more trees = more compute. Unlike Gradient Boosting, Random Forest rarely overfits with too many trees (see the gif ↓↓↓). 𝗧𝗶𝗽 𝟭: Start with [100 - 1000]. 🟢 𝗠𝗮𝘅 𝗗𝗲𝗽𝘁𝗵 (𝗺𝗮𝘅_𝗱𝗲𝗽𝘁𝗵) Controls how deep each tree can grow. Deeper trees learn more complex patterns. But too deep = risk of overfitting to noise. 𝗧𝗶𝗽 𝟮: Start with [4 - 15]. 🟢 𝗠𝗮𝘅 𝗙𝗲𝗮𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲𝘀 (𝗺𝗮𝘅_𝗳𝗲𝗮𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲𝘀) Defines how many features to consider at each split. Smaller values give better generalization. 𝗧𝗶𝗽 𝟯 - Start with: → For classification: use sqrt(n_features) → For regression: use n_features / 3 🟢 𝗠𝗶𝗻_𝘀𝗮𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲𝘀_𝘀𝗽𝗹𝗶𝘁 (𝗺𝗶𝗻_𝘀𝗮𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲𝘀_𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗳) These control the minimum data required to make a split or to be a leaf. Higher values = less complex trees. They work well to reduce overfitting and smooth out predictions. 𝗧𝗶𝗽 𝟰 - Start with: → min_sample_split: [2-8] → min_sample_leaf: [1-5] 🟢 𝗕𝗼𝗼𝘁𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗽 𝗦𝗮𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴 (𝗯𝗼𝗼𝘁𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗽) Random Forest uses bootstrap by default: sampling with replacement. Bootstrap=True usually gives better generalization. 𝗧𝗶𝗽 𝟱: start with Bootstrap=True ♻️ Repost to show your interest in ML modeling! 📌 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻 𝗔𝗱𝘃𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗱 𝗠𝗟 𝗶𝗻 𝗺𝘆 𝗠𝗟 𝗔𝗰𝗮𝗱𝗲𝗺𝘆 (𝟭𝟮𝗸+ 𝗷𝗼𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗱!): • 𝗙𝗿𝗲𝗲 ML Modeling and Design Course • 𝗙𝗿𝗲𝗲 Learning Hub & Community • 𝗙𝗿𝗲𝗲 Weekly ML Tutorials https://lnkd.in/eUey-FWM

The best AI Engineers know when to use what Here's a simple roadmap to guide you 👇 If you’re serious about NLP (basic → LLMs), these are the only books you need to backup your theory. NLP (basic to LLM) roadmap: 1️⃣ 𝗛𝗮𝗻𝗱𝘀-𝗢𝗻 𝗠𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗦𝗰𝗶𝗸𝗶𝘁-𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻, 𝗞𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘀 & 𝗧𝗲𝗻𝘀𝗼𝗿𝗙𝗹𝗼𝘄 - Aurélien Géron ↳ Covers all core ML: regression, trees, SVM, neural nets. ↳ End-to-end projects in TensorFlow & Keras. (Note: PyTorch is more popular now - but the concepts are same) 2️⃣ 𝗣𝘆𝘁𝗵𝗼𝗻 𝗡𝗮𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗟𝗮𝗻𝗴𝘂𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗖𝗼𝗼𝗸𝗯𝗼𝗼𝗸 - Zhenya Antić, PhD & Saurabh Chakravarty, Ph.D. ↳ Tokenization, n‑grams, stop‑words, stemming, TF‑IDF, BM25, NER. ↳ Hands-on with NLTK, spaCy, PyTorch, Hugging Face. ↳ word2vec, GloVe, FastText (pre-transformer must-knows). 3️⃣ 𝗡𝗮𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗟𝗮𝗻𝗴𝘂𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗲𝗿𝘀 - Lewis Tunstall, Leandro von Werra, Thomas Wolf ↳ From BERT & DistilBERT to sentence-transformers. ↳ Hugging Face workflows for classification, QA. ↳ Super clear on transformer internals. 4️⃣ 𝗛𝗮𝗻𝗱𝘀-𝗢𝗻 𝗟𝗮𝗿𝗴𝗲 𝗟𝗮𝗻𝗴𝘂𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹𝘀 - Jay Alammar & Maarten Grootendorst ↳ Build a transformer from scratch. ↳ Prompting, embeddings, RAG, eval. ↳ Function calling, modern agent pipelines. Possibly you could also add - Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch) by Raschka, PhD That's really it! (there would be some overlap of topics across the books) These books are really enough for your theoretical backing - further try to incorporate these principles in your hands-on projects. -- ♻️ Repost to if you found it helpful 💚 ➕ Join 29.000+ AI/ML builders here: https://lnkd.in/ds_SzEUH

posts.title: Abi Aryan ☯︎ View Abi Aryan ☯︎’s profile • 2nd ML Research Engineer | Author: LLMOps & GPU Engineering | Making AI Syste
posts.content: Abi Aryan ☯︎ View Abi Aryan ☯︎’s profile • 2nd ML Research Engineer | Author: LLMOps & GPU Engineering | Making AI Systems go brrrr... 5mo • 5mo Visible to everyone Someone asked me, "If you had to build a single skill roadmap for anyone, undergrads, devs, or ML engineers, to master GPU Engineering, what would it be?" So, here's what I would give them. Save this. Share it. Tag someone who needs it. 0️⃣ Math & Foundations (Don’t skip, being weak here hurts you later) - Linear Algebra: GEMM shapes, tiling logic, batching math - Memory Hierarchy Modeling: Latency vs. bandwidth vs. reuse - Roofline Model: Compute-bound vs. memory-bound diagnostics If you can’t sketch a roofline for your kernel on a napkin, start again. 1. GPU Architecture & Execution Model Master the mechanical reality: - SMs → Warps → Threads → Blocks → Occupancy - Registers → Shared Mem → L1/L2 → DRAM → Tensor Cores - Warp divergence, bank conflicts, coalescing - Streams, CUDA Graphs, async memcpy This is your mental model. 2. CUDA Programming (Write. Optimize. Profile. Repeat.) - Hand-write __global__ kernels that beat cuBLAS - Manual shared memory tiling + warp primitives (__shfl_sync, etc.) - Implement CUTLASS-style tiling from scratch - In Nsight Compute, learn to read: [ ] SM efficiency [ ] Achieved occupancy [ ] DRAM throughput [ ] Tensor core utilization If you can’t explain every bar in Nsight, you're building a blackbox again. 3. Study Kernel Libraries, not just pip install – READ THE CODE!! You must grok these repos: - CUTLASS – Tensor Core kernel framing - FlashAttention – Tiling + recompute mastery - vLLM PagedAttention – Real-world KV cache paging - Triton – Custom attention kernels in Python A common hiring manager test: “Walk me through FlashAttention’s tiling strategy.” 4. Compiler & Intermediate Layer Literacy You’ll debug what the compiler emits: - PTX → SASS (use cuobjdump, nvdisasm) - MLIR / XLA graphs → kernel mapping - Triton IR mental model Your goal should be: Trace a PyTorch graph → Triton IR → fused kernel → SASS 5. Performance Engineering Mechanics (Answer: “Why is this kernel slow?”) - Low occupancy? - Register spilling? - Non-coalesced loads? - Tensor cores idle? - Sync overhead? - Launch bound? 6. LLM Inference Workloads You must understand the workload: - KV cache layout & access patterns - Prefill vs. decode phase differences - MQA/GQA vs. MHA kernel implications - MoE routing kernels - Speculative decoding’s impact on memory 7. Tooling & Environment (learn benchmarking) Master: - Nsight Compute / Systems - cuobjdump, nvdisasm - Triton profiler - CUDA Graphs + stream debugging - Microbenchmark harnesses 8. Engineering Hygiene (so your production kernels don’t crash in prod) - Determinism vs. speed tradeoffs - Mixed precision correctness (not just speed) - Integration: PyTorch, TensorRT, JAX - Multi-GPU: NCCL collectives - Perf regression testing + codegen CI Who is this roadmap for? - CS undergrads dreaming of FAANG infra roles - ML engineers tired of framework black boxes - Kernel devs wanting to level up to LLM-scale systems and do Inference Engineering

By integrating 𝗚𝗿𝗮𝗽𝗵𝗥𝗔𝗚 and knowledge graphs, the book reveals how connected data enhances personalization, context, and decision-making in AI systems. posts.content: Pau Labarta Bajo View Pau Labarta Bajo’s profile • 3rd+ Building and teaching AI that works ​> Maths Olympian​> Father of 1.. sorry 2 kids 5mo • 5mo Visible to everyone Crash course on 𝗞𝘂𝗯𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗲𝘁𝗲𝘀 for ML Engineers Hands-on in 9 steps ↓ Kubernetes is one of the hard skills you nonstop find in job descriptions for ML engineers. Yet, it is one of the tools most ML engineers are scared of. Let me help you be less scared of Kubernetes, by deploying your first Python app. -> Special thanks to Marius Rugan for teaching me so many things 🙌 <- 𝗦𝘁𝗲𝗽 𝟭 > Install the tools > uv to create the project and manage Python dependencies. ↳ https://lnkd.in/eK6ECYXg > Docker to build and run docker images. ↳ https://lnkd.in/ePxUkPZW > kind to create a local Kubernetes cluster. ↳ https://lnkd.in/eXuHHqd8 > kubectl to interact with the Kubernetes cluster. ↳ https://lnkd.in/eKbbckgc 𝗦𝘁𝗲𝗽 𝟮 > Create the a local Kubernetes cluster We will create a cluster consisting of - 1 control plane node -> where the core Kubernetes components run - 2 worker nodes -> where the apps we will deploy will run. $ kind create cluster --config kind.yaml --name cluster-123 You can find the kind.yaml here ↳ https://lnkd.in/eW2gzpbk 𝗦𝘁𝗲𝗽 𝟯 > Write the business logic of your app For example this FastAPI server ↳ https://lnkd.in/e8ri7qw7 𝗦𝘁𝗲𝗽 𝟰 > Containerise your app with Docker We write a multi-stage Dockerfile to reduce the final image size. It has 2 stages: > builder -> where we install the project dependencies with uv and copy the code > runner -> where we run the FastAPI app 𝗦𝘁𝗲𝗽 𝟱 > Build the Docker image and run it locally (optional) $ docker build -t simple-api:v1.0.0 . 𝗦𝘁𝗲𝗽 𝟲 > Push the Docker image to the local Kubernetes cluster $ kind load docker-image simple-api:v1.0.0 𝗦𝘁𝗲𝗽 𝟳 > Deploy the app as a Kubernetes service We will need to create 2 resources: > a deployment.yaml -> which will define the pods that will run the app. In our case, we will have 3 replicas of the app. > a service.yaml -> which will define how to access the app from outside the cluster $ kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml $ kubectl apply -f service.yaml 𝗦𝘁𝗲𝗽 𝟴 > Test it works We port-forward the service to our local machine: $ kubectl port-forward svc/simple-api 5005:5000 And then we can hit the /health endpoint at http://localhost:5005/health and get the current time. $ curl http://localhost:5005/health {"status":"healthy","timestamp":"2025-02-21T15:25:55.445524"} Congratulations! You have just deployed a FastAPI app to a local Kubernetes cluster. 𝗚𝗶𝘁𝗵𝘂𝗯 𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗼 You can find all the source code in this Github repository. ↳ https://lnkd.in/eWkEUkwW ----- Hi there! posts.title: Meinolf Sellmann View Meinolf Sellmann’s profile • 2nd Creator of Optimization Solvers, Architect of the ECB Transaction
posts.content: Meinolf Sellmann View Meinolf Sellmann’s profile • 2nd Creator of Optimization Solvers, Architect of the ECB Transaction Settlement System, Inventor of Algorithms Reposted from Pedram Hooshangi-Tabrizi • 5mo • 5mo Visible to everyone Very important topic, but none of the proposed methods works in my experience. Why is that? 1. When we have multiple objectives, very quickly (you dont need many objectives) *every* solution is Pareto optimal. Meaning, you cannot make any objective better without worsening at least one other (the "at least" is the problem with Paretos). So computing a frontier becomes meaningless and memory prohibitive. 2. So we have to choose what to pursue. Said differently, we have to focus on the interesting part of the Pareto frontier. And that is decidedly *not* where one objective is through the roof and all others wither and die. That realization immediately kills the ideas of lexicographic (i.e. hierarchical) ordering or picking one to optimize while constraining the others. The whole point of the search is to find the right trade-offs between the objectives, so it is mute to ask the modeler beforehand what 'good' constraints for the other objectives would be. 3. The exchange rate between the different objectives changes with the solutions explored. Say, my objective 1 is excellent and objective 2 is in shambles right now. I will gladly accept to trade X units of 1 for Y units of 2. But now think you have a solution where 1 is awful and 2 is amazing. Now we would accept the exact opposite trade. This is why linear aggregations of objectives are a bad idea, as the post rightfully points out. So how to handle it correctly? Use InsideOpt Seeker.

posts.title: Aurimas Griciūnas View Aurimas Griciūnas’ profile • 2nd Founder @ SwirlAI • Ex-CPO @ neptune.ai (Acquired by OpenAI) • U
posts.content: Aurimas Griciūnas View Aurimas Griciūnas’ profile • 2nd Founder @ SwirlAI • Ex-CPO @ neptune.ai (Acquired by OpenAI) • UpSkilling the Next Generation of AI Talent • Author of SwirlAI Newsletter • Public Speaker 5mo • 5mo Visible to everyone A breakdown of 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗣𝗶𝗽𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀 𝗶𝗻 𝗠𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗦𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺𝘀 👇 And yes, it can also be used for LLM based systems! It is critical to ensure Data Quality and Integrity upstream of ML Training and Inference Pipelines, trying to do that in the downstream systems will cause unavoidable failure when working at scale. There is a ton of work to be done on the Data Lake or LakeHouse layer. 𝗦𝗲𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗲𝘅𝗮𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗯𝗲𝗹𝗼𝘄. 𝘌𝘹𝘢𝘮𝘱𝘭𝘦 𝘢𝘳𝘤𝘩𝘪𝘵𝘦𝘤𝘵𝘶𝘳𝘦 𝘧𝘰𝘳 𝘢 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘥𝘶𝘤𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘨𝘳𝘢𝘥𝘦 𝘦𝘯𝘥-𝘵𝘰-𝘦𝘯𝘥 𝘥𝘢𝘵𝘢 𝘧𝘭𝘰𝘸: 𝟭: Schema changes are implemented in version control, once approved - they are pushed to the Applications generating the Data, Databases holding the Data and a central Data Contract Registry. Applications push generated Data to Kafka Topics: 𝟮: Events emitted directly by the Application Services. 👉 This also includes IoT Fleets and Website Activity Tracking. 𝟮.𝟭: Raw Data Topics for CDC streams. 𝟯: A Flink Application(s) consumes Data from Raw Data streams and validates it against schemas in the Contract Registry. 𝟰: Data that does not meet the contract is pushed to Dead Letter Topic. 𝟱: Data that meets the contract is pushed to Validated Data Topic. 𝟲: Data from the Validated Data Topic is pushed to object storage for additional Validation. 𝟳: On a schedule Data in the Object Storage is validated against additional SLAs in Data Contracts and is pushed to the Data Warehouse to be Transformed and Modeled for Analytical purposes. 𝟴: Modeled and Curated data is pushed to the Feature Store System for further Feature Engineering. 𝟴.𝟭: Real Time Features are ingested into the Feature Store directly from Validated Data Topic (5). 👉 Ensuring Data Quality here is complicated since checks against SLAs is hard to perform. 𝟵: High Quality Data is used in Machine Learning Training Pipelines. 𝟭𝟬: The same Data is used for Feature Serving in Inference. Note: ML Systems are plagued by other Data related issues like Data and Concept Drifts. These are silent failures and while they can be monitored, we can’t include it in the Data Contract. Let me know your thoughts! 👇

posts.content: Pooja Jain View Pooja Jain’s profile • 3rd+ Storyteller | Lead Data Engineer@Wavicle| Linkedin Top Voice 2025,2024 | Linkedin Learning Instructor | 2xGCP & AWS Certified | LICAP’2022 6mo • 6mo Visible to everyone Is your Database Architecture is Holding You Back? Let's Fix That. Choosing the wrong database doesn’t just slow your queries—it compounds technical debt, burns budget, and limits scalability when you need it most. As data engineers, we’re drowning in options: relational, document, graph, time-series, vector databases… the list goes on. 👉 But here’s the reality: the database you choose today shapes your system’s capabilities for years. Here's a well segregated reference to explore: 𝐒𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞𝐝 𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐚𝐛𝐚𝐬𝐞 - Organized data formatted in a structured form that's easy to analyse and stored in the form of rows and columns with definite relationships. → This gets subdivided into OLTP(Relational) and OLAP(Analytics) based on the kind of transactions we prefer PostgreSQL, SQL, BigQuery and more. 𝐒𝐞𝐦𝐢-𝐒𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞 𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐚𝐛𝐚𝐬𝐞 - It includes some variability and inconsistency within data that makes it difficult to store until you don't process and organize it. → Having sources such as XML, JSON, dictionary, Entity Relationship Graph data and more. These can be further segregated as Document, Graph, Wide Columnar, Key-Value and others. 𝐔𝐧𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞𝐝 𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐚𝐛𝐚𝐬𝐞 - Unorganized, unstructured data that can be in any raw format from social media post, chats, to images, videos, unstructured log files, PDF's and more. → To handle these, we can access HDFS, S3, Blob Storage or Cloud Storage. 🔰Cloud providers offer various storage & database solutions: 𝗔𝗺𝗮𝘇𝗼𝗻 𝗪𝗲𝗯 𝗦𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗶𝗰𝗲𝘀 (𝗔𝗪𝗦)- Amazon DynamoDB, S3, Amazon ElastiCache, Amazon Kinesis, Amazon Redshift and Amazon SimpleDB 𝗚𝗼𝗼𝗴𝗹𝗲 𝗖𝗹𝗼𝘂𝗱 - Cloud Bigtable, Cloud Datastore, GCS, Firestore, BigQuery, Cloud SQL and Google Cloud Spanner 𝗠𝗶𝗰𝗿𝗼𝘀𝗼𝗳𝘁 𝗔𝘇𝘂𝗿𝗲 - Azure Cosmos DB, Azure Table Storage, Azure Redis Cache, Azure Data Lake Storage, Blob Storage, Azure DocumentDB and Azure Redis Cache Curious to know what should actually drive your decision? → Performance & Scalability – Can it handle your throughput today AND 10x growth tomorrow? → Data Model Fit – Does your data naturally map to rows, documents, nodes, or key-value pairs? → Integration Friction – How easily does it plug into your existing stack and workflows? → Total Cost of Ownership – License fees are just the start—factor in ops overhead, expertise required, and infrastructure costs. The right database isn’t about chasing trends. It’s about matching architectural patterns to real-world constraints. Image Credits: Rocky Bhatia What’s your go-to framework for database selection? Drop your approach below. 👇

How to measure? KL Divergence VS Wasserstein Distance 🔥 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻 𝗔𝗱𝘃𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗱 𝗠𝗟 𝗶𝗻 𝗺𝘆 𝗠𝗟 𝗔𝗰𝗮𝗱𝗲𝗺𝘆 (𝟭𝟭𝗸+ 𝗷𝗼𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗱!): https://lnkd.in/eUey-FWM 🟢 𝐒𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐭𝐨 𝐒𝐦𝐚𝐥𝐥 𝐃𝐢𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞𝐬: 👉 𝐊𝐋 𝐃𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞 is highly sensitive to small changes, especially near-zero probabilities, leading to large fluctuations as it penalizes areas with low or zero probability. 👉 𝐖𝐚𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐢𝐧 𝐃𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 measures the cumulative "cost" to transform one distribution into another, focusing on distances between probability masses. This approach enables smoother handling of small fluctuations, resulting in a more stable metric over time. 🟢 𝐃𝐞𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐨𝐧 𝐎𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐥𝐚𝐩: 👉 𝐊𝐋 𝐃𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞 depends heavily on overlap between distributions. As the “Production Data” shifts away from the “Reference Data,” the lack of overlap increases KL Divergence volatility 👉 𝐖𝐚𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐢𝐧 𝐃𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 is independent of overlap and can handle significant distribution shifts in shape or location. This characteristic makes it especially resilient for tracking gradual shifts in distribution. 🟢 𝐒𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐭𝐨 𝐎𝐮𝐭𝐥𝐢𝐞𝐫𝐬: 👉 𝐊𝐋 𝐃𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞 is highly responsive to outliers, as changes in the distribution tails can lead to sudden spikes or drops in values, making it more unstable in the presence of outliers. 👉 𝐖𝐚𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐢𝐧 𝐃𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞, by measuring the overall “cost” of moving the distribution, is less affected by minor tail variations or outliers. This property allows it to maintain stability, even if outliers appear in one distribution but not the other. 🟢 𝐓𝐚𝐤𝐞𝐚𝐰𝐚𝐲: 𝐖𝐚𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐢𝐧 𝐃𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 offers a more stable, interpretable measure for gradual distribution shifts, while 𝐊𝐋 𝐃𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞 can be used but requires careful handling to avoid instability. 📌 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻 𝗔𝗱𝘃𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗱 𝗠𝗟 𝗶𝗻 𝗺𝘆 𝗠𝗟 𝗔𝗰𝗮𝗱𝗲𝗺𝘆 (𝟭𝟭𝗸+ 𝗷𝗼𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗱!): • Free ML Modeling and Design Courses • Free Weekly ML Tutorials https://lnkd.in/eUey-FWM
