posts.content: Timur Bikmukhametov, PhD View Timur Bikmukhametov, PhD’s profile • 2nd Helping grow ML skills & careers in my ML Academy | World Top 3 ML LinkedIn Voice (Favikon) 6mo • 6mo Visible to everyone Bayesian Optimization for ML Model Tuning Explained in 5 simple steps 🔥 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻 𝗔𝗱𝘃𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗱 𝗠𝗟 𝗶𝗻 𝗺𝘆 𝗠𝗟 𝗔𝗰𝗮𝗱𝗲𝗺𝘆 (𝟭𝟭𝗸+ 𝗷𝗼𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗱!): https://lnkd.in/eUey-FWM 🧠 𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐁𝐚𝐲𝐞𝐬𝐢𝐚𝐧 𝐎𝐩𝐭𝐢𝐦𝐢𝐳𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧? Bayesian Optimization is an approach to finding the minimum of a black-box function using probabilistic models. 🤔 𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐝𝐨𝐞𝐬 𝐢𝐭 𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐤 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐌𝐋 𝐇𝐲𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐚𝐦𝐞𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐮𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠? 1️⃣ 𝐒𝐞𝐭𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐎𝐛𝐣𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞 Imagine we want to optimize the regularization coefficient, alpha, in a LASSO model to minimize validation error. 2️⃣ 𝐈𝐧𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐚𝐥 𝐒𝐚𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐠 We begin by selecting a few alphas at random and calculating validation errors for each. 3️⃣ 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐛𝐚𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐜 𝐌𝐨𝐝𝐞𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐠 Using these samples, we fit a probabilistic model, e.g. Gaussian Processes (see gif👇) The model estimates both the most probable error and its uncertainty for each potential alpha. This helps predict errors for untested alphas with confidence intervals. 4️⃣ 𝐔𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚𝐧 𝐀𝐜𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐅𝐮𝐧𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 The probabilistic predictions are then used in an acquisition function. We use the Lower Confidence Bound (LCB). The next hyperparameter value chosen minimizes the LCB value (see gif👇): LCB(x) = μ(x) − κ ⋅ σ(x) ↳ μ(x): Predicted mean (expected function value) ↳ σ(x): Standard deviation (model uncertainty) ↳ κ (kappa): Trade-off parameter controlling exploration vs. exploitation 5️⃣ 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐎𝐩𝐭𝐢𝐦𝐮𝐦 By choosing the point with the lowest LCB, we explore uncertain areas while focusing on promising regions, optimizing the search for the best solution. As we collect more samples, the function closely approximates the true error curve, allowing Bayesian Optimization to zero in on the minimum (see gif👇). 📌 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻 𝗔𝗱𝘃𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗱 𝗠𝗟 𝗶𝗻 𝗺𝘆 𝗠𝗟 𝗔𝗰𝗮𝗱𝗲𝗺𝘆 (𝟭𝟭𝗸+ 𝗷𝗼𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗱!): • Free ML Modeling and Design Courses • Free Weekly ML Tutorials https://lnkd.in/eUey-FWM

posts.title: Pau Labarta Bajo View Pau Labarta Bajo’s profile • 3rd+ Building and teaching AI that works ​> Maths Olympian​> Father o
posts.content: Pau Labarta Bajo View Pau Labarta Bajo’s profile • 3rd+ Building and teaching AI that works ​> Maths Olympian​> Father of 1.. sorry 2 kids 7mo • 7mo Visible to everyone I used to think the Transformer was the best architecture to build LLMs. I was wrong. Let me explain ⬇️ Don’t get me wrong. The Transformer is 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝘀𝘁 revolutionary architectural design in the deep learning space for the last 10 years. It has scaled > model size and training budgets > effective sequence length our models can process and use, and > conquered every LLM eval dataset benchmark out there. However, this is 𝗲𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴. There is never a single-best-solution-for-every-problem-out-there. Including yours. Let me explain. 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁’𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺? 🤔 In a real-world LLM project, you don’t care about model quality alone, you also care about model size as well. In general, your 𝗻𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗵-𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗿 𝗺𝗲𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗰 is a mix of (𝗮𝗰𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘆, 𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗻𝗰𝘆, 𝗺𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘀𝘂𝗺𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻) that is determined by the hardware constraints where you plan to deploy this LLM, e.g. consumer laptop, iPhone, Android... So the question is, > How can you find 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗼𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗮𝗹 architecture for your task, evaluation metric and hardware constraints? 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗼𝗹𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 🧠 The research team at Liquid AI has developed (and shared!) > a universal representation of all possible neural network architectures you can think of (called the space of Linear Input-Varying Systems) and (more importantly!) > An algorithm to find the best set of candidates from this large space of architectures (aka the 𝗦𝗧𝗔𝗥 𝗮𝗹𝗴𝗼) It is an end-2-end evolutionary algorithm in which you set your target quality and model size metrics, and STAR iteratively 1️⃣ 𝗲𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗮𝘁𝗲𝘀 their fitness by running a quick pre-training run on a subset of the data, 2️⃣ 𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗯𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀 the existing population to exploit what works. 3️⃣ 𝗺𝘂𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗲𝘀 a subset of candidate architectures to further explore the space of potential solutions until you hit the money and you get the architecture that has both a good enough quality and size metrics. This is how you find what works best for you. And as a mathematician I can only say that it is BEAUTIFUL ❤️ You can find the link to the original blog post by the Liquid AI team and the paper on the comments below ⬇️ ---- Follow me for more high-signal LLM engineering posts

posts.content: Timur Bikmukhametov, PhD View Timur Bikmukhametov, PhD’s profile • 2nd Helping grow ML skills & careers in my ML Academy | World Top 3 ML LinkedIn Voice (Favikon) 8mo • 8mo Visible to everyone "How to choose the regression metric?" MAPE vs R² vs RMSE - clear breakdown 👇 🔥 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻 𝗣𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗠𝗟 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗺𝗲 𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲: https://lnkd.in/emb4cFCS 𝗠𝗔𝗣𝗘 (𝗠𝗲𝗮𝗻 𝗔𝗯𝘀𝗼𝗹𝘂𝘁𝗲 𝗣𝗲𝗿𝗰𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗘𝗿𝗿𝗼𝗿) 🟢 Pros → 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗲𝗵𝗼𝗹𝗱𝗲𝗿-𝗙𝗿𝗶𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗹𝘆: MAPE provides errors in percentage terms, making it intuitive and easy to explain. → 𝗟𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗦𝗲𝗻𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝗢𝘂𝘁𝗹𝗶𝗲𝗿𝘀: Unlike RMSE, MAPE doesn’t “go berserk” with one or two high errors if actuals are also high. 🔴 Cons → 𝗦𝗲𝗻𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝘁𝗼 𝗡𝗲𝗮𝗿-𝗭𝗲𝗿𝗼 𝗩𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗲𝘀: MAPE can be misleading when actual values are close to zero, resulting in very high errors. → 𝗨𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗲𝘀 𝗘𝗿𝗿𝗼𝗿𝘀 𝗼𝗻 𝗟𝗮𝗿𝗴𝗲 𝗢𝘂𝘁𝗹𝗶𝗲𝗿𝘀: MAPE might understate errors for large actual values, giving a falsely optimistic accuracy. 𝗥² (𝗖𝗼𝗲𝗳𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗶𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝗗𝗲𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻) 🟢 Pros → 𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗶𝗻𝘀 𝗩𝗮𝗿𝗶𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲: R² shows the percentage of variability in the data that is captured by the model, making it easy to understand. 🔴 Cons → 𝗢𝘂𝘁𝗹𝗶𝗲𝗿 𝗦𝗲𝗻𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗶𝘁𝘆: Highly affected by extreme values, which can lead to misrepresentation. → 𝗗𝗼𝗲𝘀𝗻’𝘁 𝗜𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗘𝗿𝗿𝗼𝗿 𝗠𝗮𝗴𝗻𝗶𝘁𝘂𝗱𝗲: R² doesn’t give a clear sense of the actual error size. 𝗥𝗠𝗦𝗘 (𝗥𝗼𝗼𝘁 𝗠𝗲𝗮𝗻 𝗦𝗾𝘂𝗮𝗿𝗲𝗱 𝗘𝗿𝗿𝗼𝗿) 🟢 Pros → 𝗗𝗶𝗿𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝗘𝗿𝗿𝗼𝗿 𝗜𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁: Measures average error magnitude, with errors squared to emphasize larger discrepancies. → 𝗚𝗼𝗼𝗱 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗟𝗮𝗿𝗴𝗲 𝗗𝗲𝘃𝗶𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗶𝘀 𝗮 𝗣𝗿𝗶𝗼𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆: Suitable when minimizing significant errors is crucial, as it penalizes large deviations. 🔴 Cons → 𝗦𝗲𝗻𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝗢𝘂𝘁𝗹𝗶𝗲𝗿𝘀: RMSE can be misleading if the goal isn’t to prioritize large errors, as it heavily weights outliers. → 𝗟𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝘂𝗶𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗥𝗲𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗔𝗰𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘆: Unlike MAPE, it doesn’t provide a percentage-based view of error, which may be harder to interpret. 📌 𝗦𝘂𝗺𝗺𝗮𝗿𝘆 → 𝗠𝗔𝗣𝗘: Use for stable targets, with positive values away from zero. → 𝗥²: Best for comparing models on the same dataset or understanding the variance explained → 𝗥𝗠𝗦𝗘: Suitable for prioritizing large errors and when absolute error values in target units are most interpretable. 📌 𝗣.𝗦. 𝗕𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘄𝗮𝘆, 𝗜 𝘀𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗮𝗱𝘃𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗱 𝗠𝗟 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 (𝟵𝗸+ 𝗮𝗹𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗱𝘆 𝗷𝗼𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗱!): https://lnkd.in/emb4cFCS

posts.content: Shirin Khosravi Jam View Shirin Khosravi Jam’s profile • 2nd Sr. Data Scientist/ AI Engineer | Data Science, RAG, AI Agents, & MLOps | Germany’s Top Female Voice in AI (Favikon) 🇩🇪 | 235k+ AI/ML Community 🤯 | Opinions are my own! 8mo • 8mo Visible to everyone Stop wasting your time! LEARN 7 core AI Engineering skills 🔥 1 simple local RAG project 👇 Most “RAG” roadmaps throw too much at you. This one project helps you focus on what actually matters and it runs entirely local, no API keys, no vendor lock-in. Let’s break down the skills 👇 1️⃣ 𝗜𝗻𝗴𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗽𝗶𝗽𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲 – 𝗣𝗮𝗿𝘀𝗲, 𝗢𝗖𝗥, 𝗖𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗻 𝘁𝗲𝘅𝘁 ↳ Use PyTesseract to extract text from PDFs (even scanned ones) ↳ Clean and normalize text so it’s chunking-ready ↳ Reusable for legal docs, invoices, contracts, etc. 2️⃣ 𝗖𝗵𝘂𝗻𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗴𝗶𝗲𝘀 – 𝗙𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗻𝗮𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝘀𝗺𝗮𝗿𝘁 ↳ Apply basic fixed-size chunking logic ↳ Easy to extend to recursive or semantic chunking later ↳ Crucial for balancing retrieval quality vs. context size 3️⃣ 𝗘𝗺𝗯𝗲𝗱𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘀 – 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘁 𝘁𝗲𝘅𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝘃𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗼𝗿 𝘀𝗽𝗮𝗰𝗲 ↳ Load HuggingFace’s sentence-transformers locally ↳ No API calls = privacy + full control ↳ Try swapping models to compare vector quality 4️⃣ 𝗩𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗼𝗿 𝗗𝗕 + 𝗛𝘆𝗯𝗿𝗶𝗱 𝗥𝗲𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘃𝗮𝗹 – 𝗕𝗠𝟮𝟱 + 𝗩𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘀 ↳ Set up OpenSearch locally with both sparse & dense indexes ↳ Supports hybrid retrieval (semantic + keyword) ↳ Learn how query parsing and scoring works under the hood 5️⃣ 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗺𝗽𝘁 𝗘𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 – 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝘅𝘁-𝗮𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗤𝗔 ↳ Use simple Jinja templates to inject retrieved context into your prompt ↳ Test out different ways to phrase user queries ↳ Understand what makes an LLM answer more accurately 6️⃣ 𝗟𝗟𝗠 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗴𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 – 𝗙𝘂𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗹𝗼𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗮𝗻𝘀𝘄𝗲𝗿𝘀 ↳ Run models like llama2, mistral, or phi with Ollama ↳ No internet needed, fast iteration loop ↳ Useful for private, offline RAG setups 7️⃣ 𝗙𝗿𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗻𝗱 𝗨𝗫 – 𝗟𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁𝘄𝗲𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝗱𝗼𝗰 𝘀𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵 ↳ Built with Streamlit for easy upload + chat interface ↳ Gives users a simple way to interact with their documents ↳ Clean enough to demo to non-tech stakeholders 𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗺𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀 You don’t need 15 courses and 500 bookmarks. You need 1 solid RAG project that touches every real component. → Address a new usecase. → Want to scale? Swap Ollama for OpenAI. → Want to productionize? Swap Streamlit for FastAPI. → Want speed? Optimize chunking, indexing, caching. → Swap any components you want! Everything is modular - so you’re learning skills that transfer. You also have Jupyter Notebooks to experiment in here: The Blog → https://lnkd.in/dYfUVgsD The guide → https://lnkd.in/dsaAEqGF The code → https://lnkd.in/dXjBwX6Z Start here. Build confidence. Then scale. ♻️ Repost to help others 💙 -- If interested in learning each component deeply, we are starting "The Mother of AI" project tomorrow onwards - 30th July. Subscribe here to receive notification - https://lnkd.in/dBVBdkEG

posts.title: AI Career Roadmap 2025
posts.content: Sairam Sundaresan View Sairam Sundaresan’s profile • 3rd+ AI Engineering Leader | Author of AI for the Rest of Us | I help engineers land AI roles and companies build valuable products 8mo • 8mo Visible to everyone 80% of engineers will miss the AI wave. This roadmap gets you in the 20%. (All free or free-to-audit. Curated for impact) Phase 1: Foundation Build math, coding, and ML intuition from the ground up. 🔹 Math & Stats 🔸 3Blue1Brown – Essence of Calculus 🔸 Khan Academy – Linear Algebra, Probability & Stats 🔸 An Introduction to Statistical Learning (free PDF) 🔹 Programming & Data Skills 🔸 freeCodeCamp - Python + Data Analysis 🔸 LeetCode or HackerRank - DSA practice 🔸 Kaggle's Learn Section - NumPy, Pandas, Matplotlib 🔹 ML Foundations & Deep Learning 🔸 Andrew Ng – Machine Learning (Coursera) 🔸 Fast.ai – Practical Deep Learning 🔸 DeepLearning.AI – Deep Learning Specialization 🎯 Outcome: Understand the fundamentals of ML and implement models from scratch. Phase 2: Specialization Apply your fundamentals to different applications 🔹 Computer Vision 🔸 Stanford CS231n 🔸 UMich – Deep Learning for CV 🔹 Natural Language Processing 🔸 Stanford CS224n 🔸 Hugging Face – NLP Course 🔸 Sebastian Raschka – Build LLMs from Scratch 🔹 Reinforcement Learning 🔸 David Silver – DeepMind RL Series 🔸 OpenAI – Spinning Up RL 🔸 Hugging Face – Deep RL Course 🔹 Generative AI & LLMs 🔸 FastAI – Foundations to Stable Diffusion 🔸 MIT 6.S191 – Intro to Deep Learning 🔸 Stanford CS25 – Transformers United 🔸 Karpathy – Neural Networks Zero to Hero 🎯 Outcome: Specialize in cutting-edge fields and build a standout portfolio. Phase 3: Production Learn to ship real systems and lead production projects. 🔹 MLOps & Deployment 🔸 Full Stack Deep Learning 🔸 Stanford MLSys Seminars 🔸 Coursera – MLOps Specialization 🔹 AI Agents & Automation 🔸 Hugging Face – Agents Course 🔸 PhiloAgents – by Neural Maze 🎯 Outcome: Go beyond notebooks. Think pipelines, systems, and teams. Pro Tips 🔸 Keep an active GitHub or HF profile 🔸 Track research on Papers with Code 🔸 Join AI communities (Kaggle, Discord, HF forums) 🔸 Share what you learn (LinkedIn, tutorials, blogs) The best time to start was 10 years ago. The second-best time is now. What are you waiting for? ---- ♻️ Repost this to help someone trying to break into AI ➕ Follow me, Sairam, to learn AI the right way AI Career Roadmap 2025

posts.title: Banias Baabe View Banias Baabe’s profile • 3rd+ I teach AI Engineers the concepts and tools they need to stay ahead | AI
posts.content: Banias Baabe View Banias Baabe’s profile • 3rd+ I teach AI Engineers the concepts and tools they need to stay ahead | AI Engineer @ Netze BW 8mo • 8mo Visible to everyone Tired of burning through your budget on LLM API calls? Building with LLMs is powerful, but costs and latency can skyrocket as you scale. What if you could slash those costs and get faster responses? Try 𝗚𝗣𝗧𝗖𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗲: a semantic cache for LLM queries. It's designed to store and reuse LLM responses intelligently. Here's how it helps you win: 💰 𝗗𝗲𝗰𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘀𝗲𝗱 𝗲𝘅𝗽𝗲𝗻𝘀𝗲𝘀: Caching results reduces API calls and token counts. ⚡️ 𝗘𝗻𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗱 𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲: Get near-instant responses for similar queries. 📈 𝗜𝗺𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗱 𝘀𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆: Easily handle more users without hitting rate limits. 🛠️ 𝗔𝗱𝗮𝗽𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗱𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹𝗼𝗽𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁: Test your app without constant LLM API connections. Instead of exact-match caching, 𝗚𝗣𝗧𝗖𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗲 uses embeddings and vector stores. This means it finds and serves cached responses for semantically similar queries. Even if the wording isn't identical, you get a cache hit. 🔗 Link to repo: github(dot)com/zilliztech/GPTCache

This box shows how I think about the evolution from: • A simple LP → To a time-indexed model → To a state-based policy → To a fully tuned Cost Function Approximation (CFA) I know MILPs (CFA) and heuristics (PFA) are the most common tools in practice, so I wrote this to bring clarity while keeping it deep enough to be useful for real-world implementation. The full write-up includes: — Simulation code outline — Gurobi Optimization implementation outline — Offline & online tuning methods — Evaluation metrics — Deployment strategies If you work in decision science, OR, supply chain, or pricing, this may help you go from solving one-off problems… to designing adaptive policies that learn over time. 📝 Full article linked in the comments 👇 #operationsresearch #optimization #decisionscience #gurobi #milp #supplychain #policydesign

posts.title: Rethinking MILP as a Policy -- Embedding MILP in SDA
posts.content: Status is reachable Adam DeJans Jr. View Adam DeJans Jr.’s profile • 1st Decision Intelligence | Author | Executive Advisor 9mo • 9mo Visible to everyone New Article: "Rethinking MILP as a Policy" In most real-world applications (especially in supply chain, logistics, and planning) MILP models and heuristics dominate. We use MILP to “optimize,” and heuristics to “run the business.” What’s often missing is a unifying framework that explains how these actually function as policies, and how to structure and tune them for sequential, uncertain environments. That’s why I wrote this paper. It’s built around Warren Powell's Sequential Decision Analytics (SDA) and shows how to embed MILP inside the Cost Function Approximation (CFA) policy class. Instead of solving a one-shot problem, you solve a parameterized MILP repeatedly, treating it as a state-aware decision policy. Using Gurobi Optimization, this becomes a powerful and interpretable real-time control mechanism. 📄 What's inside: – The full SDA modeling framework (state, decision, information, transition, contribution) – How MILPs become policies via CFA – Offline + online tuning techniques – Fully worked example (inventory control under stochastic demand) – Python + Gurobi Optimization implementation – Evaluation metrics and deployment guidance I know CFA and PFA are the most common tools people already use, so this is written to add clarity, but with enough technical depth to be practically useful for PhDs and practitioners alike. 💬 I’d love your thoughts, feedback, or war stories from embedding MILP into real-time systems. Let’s push optimization forward! From static planning to living decision systems! #operationsresearch #gurobi #optimization #sequentialdecisions #MILP #decisionintelligence #supplychain #reinforcementlearning #SDA #OR #decisionmaking Rethinking MILP as a Policy -- Embedding MILP in SDA

Here's how & why👇 𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝘂𝗽𝗴𝗿𝗮𝗱𝗲? ✅ Because pip install -r is slow, messy, and breaks too often. ✅ 10-100× faster installs (essential for heavy ML pipelines) ✅ All configs in one place (no more scattered pytest.ini, .flake8, setup.py…) ✅ Exact reproducibility with uv.lock (same env on laptop, CI, prod) ✅ Lean environments - install extras only when needed ✅ This is literally Python’s future (PEP 621 + PEP 582) 𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗸 𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗶𝘁? 1️⃣ [project] → dependencies → Core prod packages (FastAPI, pandas, scikit-learn, Torch) → Minimal, production-ready ML + API stack. 2️⃣ [project.optional-dependencies] → NLP, MLOps, analytics - install only when needed: → uv pip install ".[mlops]" ".[nlp]" → Keeps project lean. 3️⃣ [dependency-groups] → Dev tools split - tests, lint, notebooks stay out of prod → Cleaner deploys, no extra baggage. 4️⃣ [tool.ruff], [tool.pytest], [tool.coverage] → All configs in the same file. → Goodbye .flake8, pytest.ini, mypy.ini clutter. 5️⃣ uv.lock → Pins exact versions. → Zero “works on my machine” excuses :D If you’re still fighting pip install -r requirements.txt, or juggling multiple config files, it’s time to switch. Listen, it is always good to be production ready. Why not start earlier if not yet started? What do you think? posts.title: 𝗥𝗲𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘃𝗮𝗹-𝗔𝘂𝗴𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗚𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻
posts.content: Shivani Virdi View Shivani Virdi’s profile • 2nd AI Engineering | Founder @ NeoSage | ex-Microsoft • AWS • Adobe | Teaching 70K+ How to Build Production-Grade GenAI Systems 9mo • 9mo Visible to everyone This is the simplest and the most complete introduction to RAG that you'll ever find. I wish I had this guide when I first started. Modern LLMs are powerful, but they’re static. They can’t access your internal docs, recent tickets, or product updates. They don’t “look up” answers. They interpolate. And when they don’t know, They hallucinate. Most real-world use cases aren’t about abstract language. They’re about your data. → What’s our refund policy? → What did the customer say last week? → What’s the latest HR guideline? So, how do you bridge that gap? You don’t need to fine-tune. You don’t need to prompt harder. You need 𝗥𝗲𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘃𝗮𝗹-𝗔𝘂𝗴𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗚𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 (𝗥𝗔𝗚). Here’s what this guide breaks down: 🔹 𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗰 𝗟𝗟𝗠𝘀 𝗳𝗮𝗶𝗹 𝗶𝗻 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 They don’t have access to real-time or proprietary data, and when left unaided, they hallucinate with confidence. 🔹 𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗺𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗳𝗶𝗻𝗲-𝘁𝘂𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗳𝗮𝗹𝗹 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝗿𝘁 Prompting only changes 𝘩𝘰𝘸 the model responds. Fine-tuning changes the weights—but it’s costly, brittle, and still static. Neither gives the model 𝘯𝘦𝘸 𝘬𝘯𝘰𝘸𝘭𝘦𝘥𝘨𝘦 in real-time. 🔹 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗥𝗔𝗚 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗶𝘀 RAG doesn’t modify the model; it modifies the input. It retrieves relevant context (docs, tickets, policies) and feeds it into the prompt at inference time. No retraining. Just better answers, grounded in your own data. 🔹 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗥𝗔𝗚 𝗹𝗼𝗼𝗽 𝗹𝗼𝗼𝗸𝘀 𝗹𝗶𝗸𝗲 𝗲𝗻𝗱-𝘁𝗼-𝗲𝗻𝗱 → Embed the user query → Perform vector search → Retrieve top-k relevant chunks → Inject those chunks into the prompt → Let the LLM generate a grounded response 🔹 𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗻𝗮𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗥𝗔𝗚 𝘀𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺𝘀 𝗳𝗮𝗶𝗹 • Bad chunking (splits mid-sentence, loses semantics) • Embeddings that don’t reflect your domain • Missing metadata filtering • Model ignoring context • Retrieval failures that sound fluent but mislead users 🔹 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗺𝗮𝗸𝗲𝘀 𝗥𝗔𝗚 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻-𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗱𝘆 ✔ Hybrid retrieval (dense + sparse) ✔ Re-ranking with cross-encoders ✔ Semantic chunking + metadata tagging ✔ Feedback loops to improve retrieval over time ✔ Monitoring retrieval quality 🔹 𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝘁𝗼 𝗲𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗮 𝗥𝗔𝗚 𝘀𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺 Using the 𝗥𝗔𝗚 𝗧𝗿𝗶𝗮𝗱: 1. 𝘙𝘦𝘵𝘳𝘪𝘦𝘷𝘢𝘭 𝘘𝘶𝘢𝘭𝘪𝘵𝘺 – Did you fetch the right chunks? 2. 𝘍𝘢𝘪𝘵𝘩𝘧𝘶𝘭𝘯𝘦𝘴𝘴 – Did the model stick to the context? 3. 𝘈𝘯𝘴𝘸𝘦𝘳 𝘘𝘶𝘢𝘭𝘪𝘵𝘺 – Was the response complete, clear, and helpful? If you’re building with LLMs, this is the system blueprint you’ll keep referring back to. ♻️ Repost to help your network upskill — 🔗 Read the full breakdown here: 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗘𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗿’𝘀 𝗚𝘂𝗶𝗱𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝗥𝗔𝗚 (Link in PDF and comments) 𝗥𝗲𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘃𝗮𝗹-𝗔𝘂𝗴𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗚𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

posts.content: Timur Bikmukhametov, PhD View Timur Bikmukhametov, PhD’s profile • 2nd Helping grow ML skills & careers in my ML Academy | World Top 3 ML LinkedIn Voice (Favikon) 9mo • 9mo Visible to everyone Never grasped how SHAP explains ML predictions? This guide makes CRYSTAL CLEAR 👇 🧠 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗦𝗛𝗔𝗣 𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗲𝘀? SHAP values quantify the contribution of each feature to a machine learning model’s prediction. This is a proven method to ensure we can trust and understand our ML models. 👇 This PDF guide explains SHAP with an easy analogy. 🟢 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝘂𝗶𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗗𝗦 𝗧𝗲𝗮𝗺𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸 𝗔𝗻𝗮𝗹𝗼𝗴𝘆 Imagine each feature is a “team member” contributing to the final team work outcome (model prediction), just like data scientists working together to solve a project. Based on calculating of each team member contribution, you will understand how features contribute to the ML models outcome. 🟢 𝗣𝗲𝗿𝗳𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗠𝗟 𝗣𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗲𝗿𝘀 If you’re building machine learning models, especially in high-stakes applications where interpretability is key, learning SHAP values is a game-changer. posts.title: Shantanu Ladhwe View Shantanu Ladhwe’s profile • 2nd Head of AI ML | 100k+ Linkedin | AI Agents, RAG, NLP, Recommenders,
posts.content: Shantanu Ladhwe View Shantanu Ladhwe’s profile • 2nd Head of AI ML | 100k+ Linkedin | AI Agents, RAG, NLP, Recommenders, Search & MLOps 9mo • 9mo Visible to everyone I have interviewed 100+ AI/ML Engineers 90% of them don't make it through ML/AI System whiteboard interview... LLM may take over programming... But AI Engineering is still 90% real engineering. After 9+ years of experience, here’s the hard truth 👇 30% of ML/AI systems fail - not because the model is bad, but because the system design is weak and engineering practices are poor. AND In 2025 and beyond, AI/ML System Design will be one of the most valuable skills in tech. Everyone’s busy exploring 10 different agentic flows and stuffing LLMs in every possible step… Until they realize: → It takes 10 seconds to generate a response → The infra couldn’t scale to traffic → It’s too costly to scale for millions of requests → Their best model can’t even be deployed without breaking infra → The team didn’t think about caching, monitoring, observability… I’ve seen amazing models fail in production because the system wasn’t built right. So if you’re serious about a long-term path in AI/ML Engineering - read these books (top → bottom) in this order. Yes, I’ve read them all. From beginner to advanced: 1️⃣ 𝗗𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗠𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗦𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺𝘀 - by Chip Huyen Perfect start for understanding real-world ML system development. 2️⃣ 𝗠𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗦𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺 𝗗𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗶𝗲𝘄 - by Ali Aminian & Alex Xu Great for structured thinking around system design & architecture for ML interviews. 3️⃣ 𝗔𝗜 𝗘𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 - by Chip Huyen Goes deep into building LLM/RAG systems, multi-modal setups, and infra choices. 4️⃣ 𝗗𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮-𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘀𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗔𝗽𝗽𝗹𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 - by Martin Kleppmann I don’t see many mention this book but it is a must-read to understand distributed systems, storage, and backend reliability. (You don’t have to read every chapter - pick what matches your use case.) posts.title: Bayesian Optimization for Hyperparameters
posts.content: Timur Bikmukhametov, PhD View Timur Bikmukhametov, PhD’s profile • 2nd Helping grow ML skills & careers in my ML Academy | World Top 3 ML LinkedIn Voice (Favikon) 10mo • 10mo Visible to everyone Clear-cut guide to Bayesian Optimization for ML Model Hyperparameters Tuning 🧠 𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐁𝐚𝐲𝐞𝐬𝐢𝐚𝐧 𝐎𝐩𝐭𝐢𝐦𝐢𝐳𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧? Bayesian Optimization is an approach to finding the minimum of a black-box function using probabilistic models. 🤔 𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐝𝐨𝐞𝐬 𝐢𝐭 𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐤 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐌𝐋 𝐇𝐲𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐚𝐦𝐞𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐮𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠? Here’s a step-by-step breakdown: 🟢 𝐒𝐞𝐭𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐎𝐛𝐣𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞 Imagine we want to optimize the regularization coefficient, alpha, in a LASSO model to minimize validation error. 🟢 𝐈𝐧𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐚𝐥 𝐒𝐚𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐠 We begin by selecting a few alphas at random, for example, 0, 3.8, 6.8, and 10, and calculating validation errors for each. 🟢 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐛𝐚𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐜 𝐌𝐨𝐝𝐞𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐠 Using these samples, we fit a probabilistic model, like Gaussian Processes, to estimate both the most probable error and its uncertainty for each potential alpha. This helps predict errors for untested alphas with confidence intervals. 🟢 𝐁𝐚𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐄𝐱𝐩𝐥𝐨𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐄𝐱𝐩𝐥𝐨𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗹𝗼𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻: Sample alphas in high-uncertainty areas to discover potentially better values. 𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗹𝗼𝗶𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻: Sample near alpha values with low error, focusing on promising regions. 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗱𝗲-𝗢𝗳𝗳: This exploration-exploitation balance is key to finding the best solution efficiently. 🟢 𝐔𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚𝐧 𝐀𝐜𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐅𝐮𝐧𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 An acquisition function, like the Lower Confidence Bound, combines estimated error and uncertainty to help select the next alpha that’s likely to have the lowest error. 🟢 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐎𝐩𝐭𝐢𝐦𝐮𝐦 As we collect more samples, the acquisition function closely approximates the true error curve, allowing Bayesian Optimization to zero in on the minimum. 🟢 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐨𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐄𝐱𝐩𝐥𝐨𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐄𝐱𝐩𝐥𝐨𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 Adjusting the trade-off parameter (in this case, kappa) allows more exploration for broader search or exploitation for finer optimization near the best-known point. ♻️ Repost to show your interest in Bayesian Optimization! P.S. Do you use BO, Random Search or Grid Search in your projects? Bayesian Optimization for Hyperparameters

posts.content: Pau Labarta Bajo View Pau Labarta Bajo’s profile • 3rd+ Building and teaching AI that works ​> Maths Olympian​> Father of 1.. sorry 2 kids 9mo • 9mo Visible to everyone I am an ML engineer who builds ML/LLM systems for a living for 9 years. This is what I found out ⬇️ Companies (still in 2025!!) struggle to find ML engineers who can design, implement and bring to life ML and LLM systems that move business metrics. This is the ML expertise that I share in my newsletter, inside the Real World ML Community on Discord and in each of my courses. ...like in my live course, Building a Real Time ML System. Together. This is the plan 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗻 I teach you how to build cars. Like real cars, not toy cars. In this case, we will build a real time ML system to predict short-term crypto prices. > I will first show you how to setup a local Kubernetes cluster with Docker (with the help of Marius Rugan), so we develop production-ready code from day 1. > The first pipeline of our system will ingest live trades from Kraken, and will produce (hopefully useful) ML model features using technical analysis. > After that, I will show you how to plot this data in real-time with Grafana. > Then we will enter the ML modelling phase, and we will write the training pipeline of our system. We will deploy it to our Kubernetes cluster and implement automatic re-training. > Once we have a model, I will show you how to produce and serve its predictions in real-time. We will implement this component in Rust, because I think this is the language you should use to write this part of the system (you will hate me a little bit for not using FastAPI here, but I promise you the effort is super worth it). Once we have this end-2-end raw-data-to-predictions system up and running, we will try to improve it. 𝗛𝗼𝘄? We will add a second source of data (in this case financial news in real-time) and transform in real-time into a crypto sentiment score, with the help of an LLM. I don’t want us to build a simple wrapper around a third-party LLM API, like OpenAI, Claude or Grok. I want us to do some real world LLM engineering, so if you zoom in into this component of the system, you will find yet-another ML system :-) (this is Compound AI, my friend), with > A feature pipeline that generates (instruction, output) datasets. > A fine-tuning pipeline that produces a light 3B-7B LLM that works well and fast > An inference pipeline using vLLM to serve the final model predictions to the rest of the infrastructure. Look, I am not going to lie to you. It will be tough. And you will need to work A LOT. But let me tell you something: If you manage to do it, you are on the top 5%. Do you accept the challenge? posts.content: Timur Bikmukhametov, PhD View Timur Bikmukhametov, PhD’s profile • 2nd Helping grow ML skills & careers in my ML Academy | World Top 3 ML LinkedIn Voice (Favikon) 10mo • 10mo Visible to everyone Data Drift in Production. How to measure? KL Divergence VS Wasserstein Distance 🔥 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻 𝗣𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗠𝗟 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗺𝗲 𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲: https://lnkd.in/emb4cFCS 🟢 𝐒𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐭𝐨 𝐒𝐦𝐚𝐥𝐥 𝐃𝐢𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞𝐬: 👉 𝐊𝐋 𝐃𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞 is highly sensitive to small changes, especially near-zero probabilities, leading to large fluctuations as it penalizes areas with low or zero probability. 👉 𝐖𝐚𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐢𝐧 𝐃𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 measures the cumulative "cost" to transform one distribution into another, focusing on distances between probability masses. This approach enables smoother handling of small fluctuations, resulting in a more stable metric over time. 🟢 𝐃𝐞𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐨𝐧 𝐎𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐥𝐚𝐩: 👉 𝐊𝐋 𝐃𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞 depends heavily on overlap between distributions. As the “Production Data” shifts away from the “Reference Data,” the lack of overlap increases KL Divergence volatility 👉 𝐖𝐚𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐢𝐧 𝐃𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 is independent of overlap and can handle significant distribution shifts in shape or location. This characteristic makes it especially resilient for tracking gradual shifts in distribution. 🟢 𝐒𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐭𝐨 𝐎𝐮𝐭𝐥𝐢𝐞𝐫𝐬: 👉 𝐊𝐋 𝐃𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞 is highly responsive to outliers, as changes in the distribution tails can lead to sudden spikes or drops in values, making it more unstable in the presence of outliers. 👉 𝐖𝐚𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐢𝐧 𝐃𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞, by measuring the overall “cost” of moving the distribution, is less affected by minor tail variations or outliers. This property allows it to maintain stability, even if outliers appear in one distribution but not the other. 🟢 𝐓𝐚𝐤𝐞𝐚𝐰𝐚𝐲: 𝐖𝐚𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐢𝐧 𝐃𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 offers a more stable, interpretable measure for gradual distribution shifts, while 𝐊𝐋 𝐃𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞 can be used but requires careful handling to avoid instability. 🔥 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻 𝗣𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗠𝗟 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗺𝗲 𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲: https://lnkd.in/emb4cFCS ♻️ Repost to show your interest in the Data Drift topic! posts.title: 5 Free Courses on Shipping AI to Production
posts.content: Paul Iusztin View Paul Iusztin’s profile • 2nd Senior AI Engineer • Founder @ Decoding AI • Author @ LLM Engineer’s Handbook ~ I ship AI products and teach you about the process. 10mo • 10mo Visible to everyone You don’t become an AI engineer by tweaking someone else’s notebook. You do it by building real systems, end-to-end. That’s exactly what these 5 open-source courses teach you to do. At Decoding ML, we were tired of surface-level tutorials that only scratched the surface of LLMs, RAG, and AI agents. So we built the kind of learning experience we wished we had when starting: - Project-based - Opinionated - Production-ready. No fake data or hand-waving over infra. Just real-world projects backed by engineering best practices: ✅ Modular Python architecture ✅ Full-stack MLOps + LLMOps ✅ RAG, agents, and evaluation systems ✅ Fine-tuning, serving, and containerization ✅ Building full-fledged end-to-end systems. And yes… you’ll need to sweat through the hard parts. Because these aren’t one-notebook tutorials or weekend demos. These are full-stack, real-world AI systems with multiple components, modular architecture, and production-level complexity. We teach you how to: - Connect custom pipelines across ingestion, retrieval, and inference - Orchestrate agents with memory, reasoning, and tool use - Containerize, serve, and version your models like a real AI engineer - Monitor, evaluate, and iterate using observability best practices Here's exactly what you'll build: 𝟭. 𝗣𝗵𝗶𝗹𝗼𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 (𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 The Neural Maze) Build a character simulation engine powered by RAG agents, memory, and real-time inference. → Learn LangGraph, RAG agents, Observability, and shipping agents as real-time APIs. 𝟮. 𝗦𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗱 𝗕𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝗔𝗜 𝗔𝘀𝘀𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗻𝘁 Chat with your knowledge base using a custom agentic RAG system. → Learn modular RAG pipelines, fine-tuning LLMs, full-stack deployment, and LLMOps. 𝟯. 𝗔𝗺𝗮𝘇𝗼𝗻 𝗧𝗮𝗯𝘂𝗹𝗮𝗿 𝗦𝗲𝗺𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗰 𝗦𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵 Build a natural language product RAG search engine for structured data. → Learn hybrid retrieval leveraging tabular data, embeddings, and metadata filtering. 𝟰. 𝗟𝗟𝗠 𝗧𝘄𝗶𝗻 Create your own digital AI replica that reflects your knowledge and communication style. → Learn LLM fine-tuning, RAG, vector DBs, and building end-to-end LLMOps systems. 𝟱. 𝗛&𝗠 𝗥𝗲𝗮𝗹-𝗧𝗶𝗺𝗲 𝗥𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿 Deploy a neural fashion recommender on Kubernetes using Hopsworks + KServe. → Learn real-time recommender systems, LLM-augmented recsys, and MLOps workflows. Everything is FREE. All you have to do is: → Clone the GitHub repo → Open the Substack lesson → Run the code + follow the guide → Remix it and build your own production AI system If you're serious about going from "learning AI" to actually shipping it, this is where to start. The link is in the comments. 5 Free Courses on Shipping AI to Production

posts.title: Benjamin Tardy View Benjamin Tardy’s profile • 2nd AI & ML Engineer 11mo • 11mo Visible to everyone Lorsque vous écrivez
posts.content: Benjamin Tardy View Benjamin Tardy’s profile • 2nd AI & ML Engineer 11mo • 11mo Visible to everyone Lorsque vous écrivez votre 𝗗𝗼𝗰𝗸𝗲𝗿𝗳𝗶𝗹𝗲, il y a des concepts importants à garder en tête pour 𝗼𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗶𝘀𝗲𝗿 𝗹’𝗶𝗺𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗴𝗲́𝗻𝗲́𝗿𝗲́𝗲. La première chose à savoir est que chaque instruction crée un 𝗻𝗼𝘂𝘃𝗲𝗮𝘂 𝗹𝗮𝘆𝗲𝗿 et que, lors du build, ces layers sont mis en cache. 🔁 Ainsi, si un layer change, tous les layers suivants doivent être reconstruits, même s'ils ne sont pas directement impactés. Cela signifie que l'ordre des instructions dans votre Dockerfile peut influencer la performance du build. Dans l’exemple 1 ci-dessous, tous les fichiers de l’application sont copiés en une seule fois dans l’image Docker. Cela implique que, si quoi que ce soit change dans ces fichiers, toutes les couches suivantes seront également reconstruites, y compris la commande pip install. ❌ Donc, même un changement mineur dans le code source, sans ajout de nouvelles dépendances, déclenchera une réinstallation complète des packages Python lors du build. ✅ C’est pourquoi il est plus judicieux de copier d’abord uniquement le fichier requirements.txt et d’exécuter ensuite le pip install (exemple 2). On peut ensuite copier l’ensemble des fichiers de l'application. De cette manière, le pip install ne sera relancé que si requirements.txt est modifié. Si vous modifiez uniquement le code source, Docker utilisera le cache et ne réinstallera pas les dépendances. ____ 🔥 Je poste (presque) tous les jours sur #python #datascience #ML #IA 📬 Veille Data/IA tous les mercredis – 15 min chrono : https://lnkd.in/dtX7Q2xB 🚀 Marre de galérer en entretien data ? yiptensor.fr t’aide à te préparer et à assurer le jour J

posts.content: Timur Bikmukhametov, PhD View Timur Bikmukhametov, PhD’s profile • 2nd Helping grow ML skills & careers in my ML Academy | World Top 3 ML LinkedIn Voice (Favikon) 10mo • 10mo Visible to everyone TOP 6 Time Series Forecasting Libraries in 2025 (with Pros and GitHub Stars) 👇 🔥 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻 𝗣𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗠𝗟 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗺𝗲 𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲: https://lnkd.in/eUey-FWM 🟢 𝗡𝗶𝘅𝘁𝗹𝗮 𝗦𝗲𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝗟𝗶𝗯𝗿𝗮𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘀 - 𝟭𝟮𝗸 ⭐ Nixtla is a set of state-of-the-art time series forecasting methods that are embedded in a set of libraries and models, most famous are: → statsforecast → neuralforecast → TimeGPT Today, Nixtla is a go-to environment to solve your time series forecasting problems. 🟢 𝗗𝗔𝗥𝗧𝗦 - 𝟴𝗸 ⭐ Darts offers a consistent 𝘧𝘪𝘵() and 𝘱𝘳𝘦𝘥𝘪𝘤𝘵() interface across various forecasting models, from classical methods like ARIMA to deep learning models. This makes it easy to compare and switch between different models without needing to understand their internal workings 🟢 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗽𝗵𝗲𝘁 - 𝟭𝟴.𝟰𝗸 ⭐ Prophet is specifically designed for users with limited statistical knowledge, allowing them to easily handle seasonal effects and missing data. Its intuitive interface makes it accessible for business applications requiring quick and interpretable forecasts. 🟢 𝗦𝗞𝗧𝗶𝗺𝗲 - 𝟳.𝟴𝗸 ⭐ SKtime provides a scikit-learn-compatible framework for time series analysis, enabling users to apply machine learning techniques seamlessly. This integration allows for easy model tuning, validation, and deployment using familiar tools. You can also easily use embedded scikit-learn data transformers for feature generation 🟢 𝗚𝗹𝘂𝗼𝗻-𝗧𝗦 - 𝟰.𝟲𝗸 ⭐ GluonTS is focused on probabilistic forecasting, allowing users to generate not just point forecasts but also confidence intervals. 🟢 𝗣𝘆𝗧𝗼𝗿𝗰𝗵 𝗙𝗼𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 – 4.6𝘬 ⭐ Built on PyTorch Lightning, PyTorch Forecasting enables flexible, interpretable, and scalable deep learning models like Temporal Fusion Transformers (TFT). Great for researchers and practitioners working on multivariate forecasting with advanced deep learning techniques. It can also be easily integrated with Amazon SageMaker, allowing users to scale their training and deployment processes efficiently. 🔥 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻 𝗣𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗠𝗟 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗺𝗲 𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲: https://lnkd.in/eUey-FWM ♻️ Repost to show your interest in Time Series Modeling! P.S. Which library do you usually use for Univariate Time Series Problems?

posts.content: Avi Chawla View Avi Chawla’s profile • 3rd+ Co-founder DailyDoseofDS | IIT Varanasi | ex-AI Engineer MastercardAI | Newsletter (150k+) 11mo • 11mo Visible to everyone 4 techniques to compress ML models for production (actively used to save 1000s of $$ in costs) Training the best-performing model is just a small part of model building. Much of our engineering effort, however, goes into making the model production-friendly. Because typically, the model that gets shipped is NEVER solely determined by performance (a misconception that many have). Instead, we also consider several operational and feasibility metrics, such as: - Inference Latency - Model size - Ease of scalability, etc. For instance, consider the results in the image below (taken from my personal experiment). It compares the accuracy and size of a large neural network with its pruned (or reduced) versions. Looking at these results, don’t you strongly prefer deploying the model that is 72% smaller, but is still (almost) as accurate as the large model? Of course, which model to proceed with still depends on various business considerations, but in many cases, it might make very little sense to deploy the large model when one of its largely pruned versions performs equally well. The techniques that help us achieve this are called model compression techniques. Four widely popular model compression techniques are: 1) Knowledge distillation: Train a large model (teacher) and transfer its knowledge to a smaller model (student). 2) Model Pruning: Remove irrelevant edges and nodes from a network. Three popular pruning techniques are zero pruning, activation pruning, and redundancy pruning. 3) Low-rank factorization: Decompose weight matrices into smaller “low-rank” matrices. 4) Quantization: Reduce the model’s memory usage by using a lower-bit representation to store parameters. I have linked an article in the comments to dive more. 👉 Over to you: Assuming you are not dealing with any sensitive use case and cost is a consideration, which model will you deploy—Model A or Model B? posts.content: Paul Iusztin View Paul Iusztin’s profile • 2nd Senior AI Engineer • Founder @ Decoding AI • Author @ LLM Engineer’s Handbook ~ I ship AI products and teach you about the process. 11mo • 11mo Visible to everyone There’s a lot of hype around AI agents. But here’s the thing nobody tells you: The hardest part isn’t building the agent... It’s stitching together the right tools to make it work in a real system. In our new PhiloAgents course (collab with Miguel Otero Pedrido), we set out to build something fun but technically solid: An interactive village of philosopher NPCs -each powered by real AI agents. And under the hood? A full-stack, real-time simulation, built with industry-grade components. Let me break down the tech stack we used to power it: - 𝗟𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗚𝗿𝗮𝗽𝗵 (by LangChain) The brain of each philosopher agent. We use it to: → Build the agentic layer → Manage state → Implement RAG pipelines that scale. - Groq (𝗟𝗹𝗮𝗺𝗮 𝟯.𝟯 𝟳𝟬𝗕) One of the fastest inference APIs we’ve tested. Helps us stream low-latency responses in real-time - perfect for interactive environments. - MongoDB Acts as both short-term and long-term memory. It stores dialogue history, philosopher knowledge bases, and retrieval indexes for contextual grounding. - 𝗙𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗔𝗣𝗜 + 𝗪𝗲𝗯𝗦𝗼𝗰𝗸𝗲𝘁𝘀 The backend layer that handles real-time communication between our agents and the game UI. Enables token-by-token streaming like ChatGPT. - 𝗣𝗵𝗮𝘀𝗲𝗿 (𝗝𝗮𝘃𝗮𝗦𝗰𝗿𝗶𝗽𝘁) The frontend engine for our game world. It’s what lets players explore, interact, and chat with thinkers from Plato to Turing - right in the browser. - 𝗢𝗽𝗶𝗸 (by Comet) Handles prompt versioning, trace monitoring, and evaluation. We track trace spans, monitor prompts, and benchmark agent performance with automated and human-aligned metrics. 𝗕𝗼𝗻𝘂𝘀: We also built a crawler + chunking + deduplication pipeline. The purpose is to gather philosophical knowledge from sources like Wikipedia + SEP, embed it, index it, and use it for hybrid RAG. I usually tell people not to obsess over tools... But in the agents world... Choosing the right stack is a survival skill. That’s why we open-sourced everything. You’ll find the architecture, lessons, and full repo in the PhiloAgents course. (Link in the comments) P.S. If you're building agentic apps and feel overwhelmed by the tool landscape, this stack might save you weeks of frustration.

posts.title: Andreas Ruf View Andreas Ruf’s profile • 3rd+ Statistician M.Sc. | Data Science & -Analysis | Theory & Real World Applic
posts.content: Andreas Ruf View Andreas Ruf’s profile • 3rd+ Statistician M.Sc. | Data Science & -Analysis | Theory & Real World Application | A.I. | (Statistical) Programming | Science Enthusiast 11mo • 11mo Visible to everyone ⚙️ The Mechanics of XGBoost ... but from a statistical point of view📚 💡The XGBoost algorithm ("Extreme Gradient Boosting") stands out in the realm of machine learning not merely for its computational efficiency, but also for its deep statistical underpinnings❗It has revolutionized machine learning with its balance of statistical rigor and computational efficiency. By analyzing its architecture and operational principles, this article will now focus on explaining XGBoost throughh the lens of its statistical foundation, shedding light on the techniques that make it an exceptionally robust and precise algorithm ✅ ⚠️ 1. We are in the field of prediction here, NOT statistical inference! ⚠️ 2. due to the limited number of strings on LinkedIn, this post is of course written in a more compact and shortened form. 🦴 The "Statistical Backbone" of XGBoost 🦴 In short again: Its foundation lies in Gradient Boosting, a technique focused on reducing prediction errors (e.g. residuals) iteratively by leveraging gradients of a loss function L --> a statistical method to minimize the difference between observed and predicted values. 💡 What sets XGBoost apart is its precise approach to error correction and model optimization: ▪️ Regularization Techniques: By incorporating L1 (Lasso) and L2 (Ridge) regularization, XGBoost mitigates the risks of overfitting, ensuring predictions generalize well across unseen data. This statistical mechanism controls model complexity, balancing accuracy and robustness. ▪️ Second-Order Optimization: The algorithm goes beyond basic gradient-based adjustments, utilizing second derivatives (The good old Hessian matrix) to refine predictions further. This facilitates faster convergence and enhances the precision of iterative improvements (in many cases... not all!). ▪️ Feature Analysis: XGBoost evaluates feature importance statistically, measuring their impact on prediction accuracy and revealing patterns crucial for informed decision-making. 🖥️ 👌 Efficient and Scalable Design 🏃‍♂️ XGBoost’s architecture is a testament to its ability to handle large datasets without compromising statistical integrity: ▪️ Sparse Data Support: Using sparse matrix representation, XGBoost efficiently processes datasets with missing values, maintaining computational speed and predictive validity. ▪️ Parallel Processing: Decision trees are constructed simultaneously, ensuring rapid execution while preserving statistical rigor. ▪️ Scalable Learning: The algorithm processes massive datasets incrementally (see: "out-of-core learning"), adapting to resource constraints while upholding statistical precision. ❓Do you use the XGBoost in your professional practice ❓ 📚 Sources: - https://lnkd.in/eCmZ7H5b - Chen, T., & Guestrin, C. (2016). XGBoost: A scalable tree boosting system. Proceedings of the 22nd ACM SIGKDD. #datascience #machinelearning #statistics #AI #data #analytics

posts.title: Best ML Pipeline Practices
posts.content: Timur Bikmukhametov, PhD View Timur Bikmukhametov, PhD’s profile • 2nd Helping grow ML skills & careers in my ML Academy | World Top 3 ML LinkedIn Voice (Favikon) 11mo • 11mo Visible to everyone Data Scientists HAVE TO master ML pipelines. These DS mistakes can break ML pipelines: ↳ Using ambiguous library versions ↳ Ignoring model monitoring ↳ Overlooking data drifts 🔴 These mistakes lead to: ↳ Non-reproducible pipelines that fail unpredictably. ↳ Inability to detect and debug performance issues. ↳ Model degradation due to unaddressed data drift. 🟢 Instead, follow these best practices: → Pin library versions explicitly (e.g., scikit-learn==1.2.2) in requirements.txt or environment.yaml → Track model accuracy for every prediction with your module or using tools like Evidently, Neptune, or Weights & Biases → Monitor data drift with univariate and multivariate methods with your module or using tools like Evidently or NannyML. Don’t excuse yourself with: ↳ "The library versions don’t matter." ↳ "I’ll monitor performance later." ↳ "Data drift doesn’t impact my model." Best practices make pipelines reliable, reproducible, and scalable for production environments. ♻️ Repost to show your interest in ML Pipeline Best Practices! P.S. posts.content: Timur Bikmukhametov, PhD View Timur Bikmukhametov, PhD’s profile • 2nd Helping grow ML skills & careers in my ML Academy | World Top 3 ML LinkedIn Voice (Favikon) 1yr • 1yr Visible to everyone TOP 7 ML Models for Uncertainty Estimation (with Pros and Cons) 👇 🔥 Learn 𝗔𝗱𝘃𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗱 𝗠𝗟 & 𝗴𝗲𝘁 𝟮𝟯𝟬+ 𝗽𝗮𝗴𝗲𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝗩𝗶𝘀𝘂𝗮𝗹 𝗠𝗟 𝗟𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗼𝗻𝘀 here: https://lnkd.in/emb4cFCS 🟢 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗮𝗹 𝗣𝗿𝗲𝗱𝗶𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 → Produces calibrated prediction intervals based on past errors. 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝘀: Model-agnostic and provides valid coverage guarantees. 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘀: Computational cost increases for large datasets. 🟢 𝗚𝗮𝘂𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗮𝗻 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗲𝘀 (𝗚𝗣𝘀) → A non-parametric Bayesian model that provides uncertainty via covariance functions. 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝘀: Provides well-calibrated uncertainty with theoretical guarantees. 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘀: Not scalable to large datasets. 🟢 𝗤𝘂𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗹𝗲 𝗥𝗲𝗴𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 → Predicts conditional quantiles instead of a mean estimate. 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝘀: Simple, interpretable, and non-parametric. 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘀: Needs multiple models for different quantiles; doesn't capture epistemic uncertainty. 🟢 𝗕𝗮𝘆𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗮𝗻 𝗟𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗮𝗿 𝗥𝗲𝗴𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 → Estimates a posterior distribution over model parameters. 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝘀: Prevents overfitting and gives uncertainty grounded in Bayes’ rule. 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘀: Inference is slow and sensitive to prior choice. 🟢 𝗠𝗮𝗿𝗸𝗼𝘃 𝗖𝗵𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝗠𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲 𝗖𝗮𝗿𝗹𝗼 (𝗠𝗖𝗠𝗖) → Sampling-based technique for approximating posterior distributions. 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝘀: Flexible and asymptotically exact. 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘀: Very slow, especially in high dimensions. 🟢 𝗡𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘇𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗙𝗹𝗼𝘄𝘀 → Learns complex posteriors by transforming simple distributions through invertible functions. 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝘀: Scalable and supports exact density evaluation. 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘀: Hard to design; inference can be unstable. 🟢 𝗩𝗮𝗿𝗶𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗜𝗻𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲 (𝗩𝗜) → Approximates complex posteriors by optimizing a simpler distribution. 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝘀: Fast and scalable to large datasets and neural networks. 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘀: Can underestimate uncertainty; quality depends on the approximation family. 🔥 Learn 𝗔𝗱𝘃𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗱 𝗠𝗟 & 𝗴𝗲𝘁 𝟮𝟯𝟬+ 𝗽𝗮𝗴𝗲𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝗩𝗶𝘀𝘂𝗮𝗹 𝗠𝗟 𝗟𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗼𝗻𝘀 here: https://lnkd.in/emb4cFCS ♻️ Repost to show your interest in Advanced ML! posts.title: When not to use Random Forest
posts.content: Timur Bikmukhametov, PhD View Timur Bikmukhametov, PhD’s profile • 2nd Helping grow ML skills & careers in my ML Academy | World Top 3 ML LinkedIn Voice (Favikon) 1yr • 1yr Visible to everyone 4 cases when NOT to use Random Forest (that'll save you 50% of ML modeling time) 🔥 Learn 𝗔𝗱𝘃𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗱 𝗠𝗟 & 𝗴𝗲𝘁 𝟮𝟯𝟬+ 𝗽𝗮𝗴𝗲𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝗩𝗶𝘀𝘂𝗮𝗹 𝗠𝗟 𝗟𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗼𝗻𝘀 here: https://lnkd.in/emb4cFCS 🟢 𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗳𝗲𝗮𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗮𝗿𝗴𝗲𝘁 𝗿𝗲𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗽𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝘀𝘁𝗹𝘆 𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗮𝗿 In this case, Random Forest will barely outperform Linear or Logistic Regression. 👉 Linear models: ↳ Train faster ↳ Are easier to tune ↳ Are more interpretable 🟢 𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗶𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝗶𝘀𝘆, 𝘀𝗽𝗮𝗿𝘀𝗲, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗵𝗮𝘀 𝗹𝗼𝘄 𝘃𝗮𝗿𝗶𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆 Random Forest likes when: ↳ Data having many distinct feature values ↳Low noise levels For noisy and sparse data, simpler models (e.g., Linear Regression) often perform just as well. 🟢 𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹 𝗲𝘅𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗽𝗼𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗶𝘀 𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗮𝗻𝘁 Random Forest doesn’t extrapolate well. 👉 Use smooth non-linear models instead: ↳ Neural Networks ↳ Gaussian Processes 🟢 𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗻 𝘁𝗼 𝘂𝘀𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗼𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗶𝘇𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 Random Forest’s piecewise constant structure makes optimization gradients noisy and unstable. 👉 In this case, use smooth non-linear models: ↳ Neural Networks ↳ Gaussian Processes ↳ Splines 🔥 Learn 𝗔𝗱𝘃𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗱 𝗠𝗟 & 𝗴𝗲𝘁 𝟮𝟯𝟬+ 𝗽𝗮𝗴𝗲𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝗩𝗶𝘀𝘂𝗮𝗹 𝗠𝗟 𝗟𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗼𝗻𝘀 here: https://lnkd.in/emb4cFCS ♻️ Repost to show your interest in Practical Machine Learning! posts.title: Breaking Down ML Models Data Drift
posts.content: Timur Bikmukhametov, PhD View Timur Bikmukhametov, PhD’s profile • 2nd Helping grow ML skills & careers in my ML Academy | World Top 3 ML LinkedIn Voice (Favikon) 1yr • 1yr Visible to everyone Why Data Drift in ML Production Matters? Explained with a simple real-world example 👇 🌱 𝗦𝗰𝗲𝗻𝗮𝗿𝗶𝗼: 𝗖𝗼𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗲 𝗥𝗼𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗢𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗶𝘇𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 Imagine you’re using an ML model to optimize roast temperature and predict humidity for roasted coffee beans. The model uses: ↳ Bean size ↳ Inlet humidity (initially stable) ↳ Applied temperature At first, the model keeps the outlet bean humidity within the target range (10-15%). However, over time, bean size changes affect the roasting process. 🔍 𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗗𝗿𝗶𝗳𝘁 𝗜𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘀 𝗬𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹 𝗔𝗰𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘆 𝗗𝗿𝗼𝗽𝘀: As input data shifts, the model’s predictions become less reliable, impacting product quality. 𝗗𝗲𝗹𝗮𝘆𝗲𝗱 𝗗𝗲𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻: Since humidity is only measured every 12 hours, drift might go unnoticed. A drift monitoring system, however, flags shifts in real-time. 𝗖𝗼𝘀𝘁𝗹𝘆 𝗘𝗿𝗿𝗼𝗿𝘀: Incorrect roasting parameters due to drift lead to out-of-spec product, resulting in wasted batches and lost revenue. 🧩 𝗠𝗼𝗻𝗶𝘁𝗼𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗱𝗿𝗶𝗳𝘁 𝗵𝗲𝗹𝗽𝘀 𝘆𝗼𝘂: ↳ Detect data shifts early and adjust the model or process accordingly. ↳ Quickly understand if issues are due to data changes, process variations, or sensor errors. ↳ Know when it’s time to retrain the model for continued accuracy. 🟢 𝗧𝗮𝗸𝗲𝗮𝘄𝗮𝘆𝘀: ↳ Data drift is the gradual shift in statistical properties of input data, impacting model accuracy. ↳ Continuous monitoring catches shifts early, reducing costly delays in identifying performance issues. ↳ If you’re a Data Scientist or ML Engineer, data drift monitoring is key to deploying robust models. ♻️ Repost to show your interest in Production ML Topics. P.S. Do you think data drift is an important ML topic? Breaking Down ML Models Data Drift

𝗙𝗶𝗻𝗱 𝗮 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹-𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗹𝗱 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗶𝗻 Working on projects is harder than completing online courses. But hey, no pain no gain. You must work on a problem you are interested in. Otherwise, you will quit. 𝗦𝘁𝗲𝗽 𝟮. 𝗙𝗶𝗻𝗱 𝗮 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝘀𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗰𝗲 Preferably a live API. If not possible, pick a static dataset from Kaggle. Here is a superb repo with a list of public APIs you can use https://lnkd.in/dgUABbqt 𝗦𝘁𝗲𝗽 𝟯. 𝗕𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱 𝗮 𝘀𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝗠𝗟 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹 Do not try to build THE PERFECT model, and only then move to the next phase. Because this leads you to a never-ending Jupyter-notebook-development-cycle, and you get lost. Start with basic features and a basic model. And move to the next step. 𝗦𝘁𝗲𝗽 𝟰. 𝗣𝘂𝘀𝗵 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗰𝗼𝗱𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝗮 𝗽𝘂𝗯𝗹𝗶𝗰 𝗚𝗶𝘁𝗛𝘂𝗯 𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗼 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘄𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗲 𝗮 𝗯𝗲𝗮𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗳𝘂𝗹 𝗥𝗘𝗔𝗗𝗠𝗘 The README file is the first thing your future employer will see. posts.content: Timur Bikmukhametov, PhD View Timur Bikmukhametov, PhD’s profile • 2nd Helping grow ML skills & careers in my ML Academy | World Top 3 ML LinkedIn Voice (Favikon) 1yr • 1yr Visible to everyone Top 5 libraries to explain ML models (that can actually help) 🔥 More of 𝗔𝗱𝘃𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗱 𝗠𝗟 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗺𝗲 here: https://lnkd.in/emb4cFCS 🟢 𝐒𝐇𝐀𝐏 (𝐒𝐇𝐚𝐩𝐥𝐞𝐲 𝐀𝐝𝐝𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐞𝐱𝐏𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬) Most popular method and often does a decent job. The SHAP algorithm considers additive feature importance for explaining the collective contribution of the underlying model features. 🟢 𝐋𝐈𝐌𝐄 (𝐋𝐨𝐜𝐚𝐥 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐩𝐫𝐞𝐭𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐌𝐨𝐝𝐞𝐥-𝐚𝐠𝐧𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐜 𝐄𝐱𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬) Similar to SHAP, LIME is a model-agnostic explanation technique. It is used for interpreting models by learning a local model around the predictions which means it is a “local” model explainer. 🟢 𝐄𝐥𝐢5 (𝐄𝐱𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐢𝐧 𝐋𝐢𝐤𝐞 𝐈’𝐦 𝐅𝐢𝐯𝐞) Eli5 is a Python XAI library for debugging, inspecting, and explaining ML classifiers. It explains black-box models in the most simplified format and supports a wide range of ML modeling frameworks, e.g. scikit-learn and Keras. 🟢 𝐀𝐈 𝐄𝐱𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝟑𝟔𝟎 (𝐀𝐈𝐗𝟑𝟔𝟎) AIX360 is an IBM-developed open-source library designed to enhance model interpretability across multiple data types, including tabular, text, image, and time-series data. It provides a diverse set of explanation techniques and evaluation metrics, helping users assess model transparency and debug complex AI systems. 🟢 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐩𝐫𝐞𝐭𝐌𝐋 Microsoft's InterpretML is a powerful Python package offering both interpretable "glassbox" models and explainers for "blackbox" models. It helps machine learning practitioners understand model behavior using cutting-edge interpretability methods, promoting responsible AI development. ♻️ Repost to network to show your interest in ML Interpretability! 🔥 More of 𝗔𝗱𝘃𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗱 𝗠𝗟 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗺𝗲 here: https://lnkd.in/emb4cFCS P.S. posts.content: Pau Labarta Bajo View Pau Labarta Bajo’s profile • 3rd+ Building and teaching AI that works ​> Maths Olympian​> Father of 1.. sorry 2 kids 1yr • 1yr Visible to everyone Want to build a Real Time ML System in 15 minutes with me? Let's do it ↓ Real Time ML is all about building predictive systems that adapt VERY fast to changes in the underlying patterns. 𝗙𝗼𝗿 𝗲𝘅𝗮𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲 💁 Every time your credit card is used online by someone (hopefully you), your card issuer (for example Visa, MasterCard or Paypal) has to verify if it is you the person trying to pay with the card. But the question is: “How does Visa do that?” And the answer is… a real time ML system! 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁'𝘀 𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗵𝗼𝗼𝗱? 🔎 As any ML system that has existed, exists and will exist, this one can be broken down into 3 types pipelines > 𝗙𝗲𝗮𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 pipelines → produce ML model features from raw data > 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 pipeline → produce ML models from features (and targets, if you do supervised ML, which is by far the most useful one). > 𝗜𝗻𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲 pipeline → produce predictions from an ML model and fresh features. Now, credit card fraud patterns are very dynamic. Fraudsters are constantly coming up with new ways to defraud credit card companies, so your ML system needs to adapt o these changes, to keep up with the latest fraud trends To accomplish this, you: 1️⃣ Use historical data to train a good initial model. This is called, 𝗼𝗳𝗳𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴. 2️⃣ 𝗗𝗲𝗽𝗹𝗼𝘆 this model either as a streaming job, or as a REST API, so it can start making predictions on new data. 3️⃣ 𝗠𝗼𝗻𝗶𝘁𝗼𝗿 to the model, so you can detect if it's performing poorly. 4️⃣ Update the model parameters incrementally as new pairs (input, label) come in. This technique is called 𝗼𝗻𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴. The updated is redeployed frequently, to keep up with the latest fraud trends. But the thing is, building the underlying MLOps platform that supports these workflows is no piece of cake. So the question is: How do you build a production-ready real time ML system, without spending years building the underlying platform❓ And here is when TurboML comes to the rescue! 𝗦𝗼𝗹𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 🧠 In this video you will learn how to build, deploy and monitor a real-time ML system to predict credit card fraud. Feel free to adjust to the code your problem. 𝗚𝗶𝘁𝗵𝘂𝗯 𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗼 👩‍💻 I've created a hands-on example (GitHub repo linked in comments) that shows you how to: 1️⃣ Set up a development environment using devcontainers 2️⃣ Create feature pipelines for fraud detection 3️⃣ Deploy an ML model that adapts to evolving fraud patterns 4️⃣ Generate live predictions 5️⃣ Monitor model performance and compare different approaches Sign up for FREE at 𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗯𝗼𝗺𝗹.𝗰𝗼𝗺 and git clone the repo you will find on the comments below 👇

posts.content: Alex Razvant View Alex Razvant’s profile • 2nd Senior AI Engineer | Writing The AI Merge Newsletter | Helping Engineers Build AI Beyond Demos 1yr • 1yr Visible to everyone If you're still using FastAPI to deploy Hugging Face LLMs/VLMs - switch to LitApi! FastAPI is a great framework for implementing RESTful APIs. However, it wasn’t specifically designed to handle the complex requirements of serving ML models at scale. The team at Lightning AI is behind LitServe and LitApi to fill in that gap. 🔹 𝗟𝗶𝘁𝗔𝗣𝗜 builds on top of FastAPI, adapting for ML workloads, standardizes the core steps of serving a model. 🔹 𝗟𝗶𝘁𝗦𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗲𝗿 handles the infrastructure side of serving models. 🔸 Here's what you must know: 1. 𝗢𝗻𝗲-𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹 𝘀𝗲𝘁𝘂𝗽 In the 𝙨𝙚𝙩𝙪𝙥() method, we can load any model only once. 2. 𝗖𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗺𝗶𝘇𝗲 𝗣𝗿𝗲𝗱𝗶𝗰𝘁 In the 𝙥𝙧𝙚𝙙𝙞𝙘𝙩() method, we implement the inference on inputs logic. 3. 𝗖𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗺𝗶𝘇𝗲 𝗕𝗮𝘁𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗟𝗼𝗴𝗶𝗰 You can specify a MAX_BATCH_SIZE and a BATCH_TIME_WINDOW and it'll automatically handle the dynamic batching of requests as they come in concurrently. You can use ThreadPoolExecutor to parallelize the preprocessing steps in the 𝙗𝙖𝙩𝙘𝙝() method. 4. 𝗖𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗺𝗶𝘇𝗲 𝗨𝗻𝗯𝗮𝘁𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗟𝗼𝗴𝗶𝗰 After inferencing on a batch, you'll handle the detach () of GPU tensors and post-process the raw logits in the 𝙪𝙣𝙗𝙖𝙩𝙘𝙝() method. 5. 𝗗𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗱𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗾𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗼𝗱𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗽𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗲 In the 𝙙𝙚𝙘𝙤𝙙𝙚_𝙧𝙚𝙦𝙪𝙚𝙨𝙩() - specify how the API should access the input value from the request. In the 𝙚𝙣𝙘𝙤𝙙𝙚_𝙧𝙚𝙨𝙥𝙤𝙣𝙨𝙚() - specify how the API should return responses to the client. Simple as that! To scale this up for a production workload, you'll use LitServe's scale configuration parameters: ``` LitServer( lit_api: LitAPI, accelerator: str = "auto", devices: Union[str, int] = "auto", workers_per_device: int = 1, timeout: Union[float, bool] = 30, max_batch_size: int = 1, batch_timeout: float = 0.0, stream: bool = False, ) ``` 📙 For a full tutorial, see this article: https://lnkd.in/dGUrVX7s --- #machinelearning #deeplearning #artificialintelligence --- 💡 Follow me for more 𝗲𝘅𝗽𝗲𝗿𝘁 𝗶𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁𝘀 on AI/ML Engineering

posts.content: Benjamin Tardy View Benjamin Tardy’s profile • 2nd AI & ML Engineer 1yr • 1yr Visible to everyone 𝗔𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗾𝘂𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘃𝗼𝘂𝘀 𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘀𝗲𝘇 𝘂𝗻𝗲 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗹𝗼𝗴 ! Elle marche bien sur certaines distributions... mais pas sur toutes ! La log transformation est un super outil en data science. ➭ Elle permet de réduire l’asymétrie d’une distribution et de la rapprocher d’une gaussienne, ce qui bénéficie, en général, aux modèles de machine learning. 🔴 Mais elle a un défaut… Elle ne fonctionne bien que sur les distributions "right-skewed". Et si tu l’appliques sans réfléchir sur des distributions "left-skewed", tu risques d’aggraver la situation. Voici pourquoi 👇 Une distribution left-skewed (asymétrie à gauche) a une longue queue à gauche. Elle contient quelques valeurs très basses et beaucoup de valeurs élevées. ❌ Si on applique un log directement : 1⃣ Problème des valeurs négatives → Le logarithme n'est pas défini pour x < 0, ce qui rend la transformation impossible si la distribution contient des valeurs négatives. 2⃣ Effet sur les petites valeurs positives → Pour les valeurs entre 0 et 1, le logarithme donne des résultats négatifs (log(0.1) = -1, log(0.01) = -2, etc.). Cela étire la queue gauche au lieu de la comprimer, aggravant potentiellement l'asymétrie. 𝗥𝗲́𝘀𝘂𝗹𝘁𝗮𝘁 ? Au lieu de corriger l'asymétrie à gauche, la transformation logarithmique peut créer une forte asymétrie à droite, inversant le problème au lieu de le résoudre. 🚀 Alors, que faire sur une distribution left-skewed ? Il existe d’autres solutions : ✅ Box-Cox : Une transformation plus flexible qui cherche automatiquement la meilleure correction d’asymétrie. ✅ Yeo-Johnson : Une variante qui fonctionne même avec des valeurs négatives et nulles. ✅ Miroir + Log : Retourner la distribution, appliquer log, puis ré-inverser… mais ça change l’interprétation des valeurs. ___ 🕵️‍♂️ 𝗝𝗲 𝗳𝗮𝗶𝘀 𝗹𝗮 𝘃𝗲𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗲 𝗽𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝘃𝗼𝘂𝘀 : 15 minutes top chrono tous les mardis (ou mercredis) matins pour rester à la pointe des nouveautés en matière de data science, machine learning et IA avec ma 𝗻𝗲𝘄𝘀𝗹𝗲𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿 : lien sur mon profil ! posts.content: Banias Baabe View Banias Baabe’s profile • 3rd+ I teach AI Engineers the concepts and tools they need to stay ahead | AI Engineer @ Netze BW 1yr • 1yr Visible to everyone Are you still using SHAP for explaining Machine Learning models? Then it's time to switch to 𝗦𝗛𝗔𝗣-𝗜𝗤. Shapley values became very popular due to distributing effects of features fairly. One problem with it: Standard SHAP compresses complex feature interactions into single values, obscuring how features truly influence predictions together. You're missing crucial insights about your model's behavior. Shapley Interactions, on the other side, enhance the traditional Shapley value approach by providing detailed measurements for every meaningful feature combination. Now, you will not get a single value per feature, but a number for each combination of features. 𝗦𝗛𝗔𝗣-𝗜𝗤 (Shapley Interaction Quantification) is the Python package you need to explain your models. Check it out: github(dot)com/mmschlk/shapiq

posts.content: Benjamin Tardy View Benjamin Tardy’s profile • 2nd AI & ML Engineer 1yr • 1yr Visible to everyone 𝗟𝗲 𝗰𝗹𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴, 𝗰’𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝘀𝘆𝗺𝗽𝗮… jusqu’à ce qu’on doive 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘂𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝗾𝘂’𝗶𝗹 𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗯𝗼𝗻. Contrairement à la classification supervisée, il n'y a pas de moyen universel d'évaluer un clustering. Voici un mini guide pour faire les bons choix ! 𝗟'𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗹𝘆𝘀𝗲 𝗻𝘂𝗺𝗲́𝗿𝗶𝗾𝘂𝗲 𝗱𝗲 𝘃𝗼𝘀 𝗰𝗹𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗲 : Silhouette Score (proche de 1 = bien) : ✅ Atout : idéal pour des clusters convexes et denses. ⚠️ Limite : échoue sur les structures complexes et pénalise les petits clusters. Davies-Bouldin (plus faible = mieux) : ✅ Atout : bon pour comparer des clusterings sur un même jeu de données. ⚠️ Limite : sensible aux déséquilibres de densité (un cluster dense peut masquer un mauvais découpage). Indice de Dunn (plus élevé = mieux) : ✅ Atout : utile pour détecter des clusters bien séparés. ⚠️ Limite : très vulnérable au bruit (une seule observation aberrantes fausse la distance inter-cluster). Calinski-Harabasz (score élevé = mieux) : ✅ Atout : rapide à calculer pour les grands datasets. ⚠️ Limite : biaisé vers les clusters sphériques (comme k-means) et suppose une distribution gaussienne. Le problème : ces métriques sont souvent incohérentes entre elles, contrairement à ce que l'illustration pourrait faire croire. 𝗔𝗹𝗼𝗿𝘀 𝘃𝗼𝘂𝘀 𝗽𝗼𝘂𝘃𝗲𝘇 𝘃𝗼𝘂𝘀 𝘁𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗻𝗲𝗿 𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗹𝗮 𝘃𝗶𝘀𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘀𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 (𝘁-𝗦𝗡𝗘 / 𝗨𝗠𝗔𝗣) : ✅ Atout : détecte des motifs non linéaires visuellement (ex: regroupements en "îlots"). ⚠️ Limites : 👉 Les distances sont déformées → un cluster visuellement séparé peut être artificiel. 👉 La perplexité (t-SNE) ou le nombre de voisins (UMAP) influencent radicalement le résultat. 𝗟𝗮 𝗿𝗼𝗯𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗲 𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗮𝘂𝘀𝘀𝗶 𝘂𝗻 𝗰𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗲̀𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗮𝗻𝘁 : Un clustering n’est pas robuste si… → Il change radicalement avec une initialisation aléatoire différente (ex: k-means). → Il est sensible au bruit ajouté. → Les frontières des clusters sont floues Vous pouvez tester la stabilité via bootstrap ou par des approches comme le consensus clustering. 𝗘𝘃𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗺𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗹𝗮 𝘃𝗮𝗹𝗶𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗺𝗲́𝘁𝗶𝗲𝗿 𝗷𝗼𝘂𝗲 𝘂𝗻 𝗿𝗼̂𝗹𝗲 𝗺𝗮𝗷𝗲𝘂𝗿 : → Vous devez présenter les caractéristiques clés des clusters (moyennes, variables discriminantes). → Proposez des noms interprétables (ex: "Clients à fort potentiel mais faible fidélité"), ce qu'on peut aussi appeler les "personae". ___ 🕵️‍♂️ 𝗝𝗲 𝗳𝗮𝗶𝘀 𝗹𝗮 𝘃𝗲𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗲 𝗽𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝘃𝗼𝘂𝘀 : 15 minutes top chrono tous les mardis (ou mercredis) matins pour rester à la pointe des nouveautés en matière de data science, machine learning et IA avec ma 𝗻𝗲𝘄𝘀𝗹𝗲𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿 : lien sur mon profil ! posts.title: Slides mise en production, séances 2 et 3
posts.content: Lino Galiana View Lino Galiana’s profile • 3rd+ Data Scientist - Administrateur INSEE 1yr • 1yr Visible to everyone Bonnes pratiques pour mettre en production des projets de #datascience: cela ne concerne pas que le code ! 🚀 Après une première séance consacrée à sensibiliser aux enjeux d'un code propre, le cours de mise en production que Romain Avouac et moi donnons à l'ENSAE Paris s'attaque aux autres fondements nécessaires à toute mise en production. L'un des objectifs principaux de ce cours est de faire comprendre qu'une chaine de production de données peut être vue comme la combinaison de trois inputs, pour lesquels on va choisir des technologies adaptées: 👉️ Du #code: #Python comme langage principal, faisant l'interface entre d'autres briques plus spécialisées, #Git pour le contrôle de version. 👉️ De la #configuration: des paramètres qui jouent sur le résultat du code, l'environnement de reproductibilité, etc. Les extraire du code permet de mieux contrôler ce qui est confidentiel ou non, ce qui affecte les résultats ou pas, etc. 👉️ Des #données: c'est logiquement l'input de tout projet #data. Choisir formats et lieux de stockage adaptés est primordial pour l'efficacité et l'évolutivité de la chaîne. La règle d'or : pas de données dans #Git 👮! 🧠 Dans la partie magistrale, on se concentre sur les données pour parler de l'intérêt du système de stockage #cloud de type #S3, du format de données #Parquet (oui on adore Parquet à l'Insee!) et de l'écosystème associé, notamment Apache Arrow et DuckDB 🦆. La prochaine séance sera consacrée à la configuration de l'environnement de reproductibilité à travers les enjeux des environnements virtuels et de la conteneurisation. 🔧 Dans la partie pratique, l'objectif est de continuer à construire une chaîne à l'architecture modulaire. Cela facilite les choix techniques adaptés. En consacrant un temps important à ces bonnes pratiques, on essaie de montrer qu'en les adoptant dès le début, on gagne beaucoup de temps pour pouvoir réaliser des projets reproductibles ambitieux. Grâce à ces fondements, on pourra passer dans les prochaines séances à la partie mise en production à proprement parler dans les prochaines séances: conteneurisation, automatisation, déploiement d'applications, monitoring d'un projet dans une optique #MLOps, etc. Avec ces idées en tête, on fait des choix techniques et organisationnels pertinents pour construire des projets plus simples à maintenir dans le temps, plus évolutifs, plus reproductibles et qui se diffusent à plus grande échelle. C'est donc tout bénef ! 😉 Slides mise en production, séances 2 et 3

posts.content: Brij kishore Pandey View Brij kishore Pandey’s profile • 2nd AI Architect & Engineer | AI Strategist 1yr • 1yr Visible to everyone Not all APIs are created equal. Choosing the right API design can make or break your application's scalability, performance, and efficiency. 𝗛𝗲𝗿𝗲’𝘀 𝗮 𝗯𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗸𝗱𝗼𝘄𝗻 𝗼𝗳 𝘀𝗶𝘅 𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗔𝗣𝗜 𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲𝘀 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝘁𝗲𝗰𝗵 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗳𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗸𝗻𝗼𝘄: 𝗥𝗘𝗦𝗧 (𝗥𝗲𝗽𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗳𝗲𝗿) • 𝗕𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗳𝗼𝗿: Simple, resource-oriented applications • 𝗪𝗵𝘆? REST is stateless and follows standard HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE), making it easy to implement, scalable, and perfect for CRUD operations in web apps. 𝗚𝗿𝗮𝗽𝗵𝗤𝗟 • 𝗕𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗳𝗼𝗿: Flexible, efficient data fetching • 𝗪𝗵𝘆? Unlike REST, GraphQL allows clients to request only the needed data—no more, no less. This minimizes over-fetching and under-fetching, making it a game-changer for front-end-heavy applications with complex data structures. 𝗦𝗢𝗔𝗣 (𝗦𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝗢𝗯𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝗔𝗰𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝘁𝗼𝗰𝗼𝗹) • 𝗕𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗳𝗼𝗿: High-security, enterprise applications • 𝗪𝗵𝘆? SOAP is XML-based and built with strict security standards, making it ideal for industries like banking and healthcare that require ACID compliance and robust security protocols. 𝗴𝗥𝗣𝗖 (𝗚𝗼𝗼𝗴𝗹𝗲 𝗥𝗲𝗺𝗼𝘁𝗲 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗰𝗲𝗱𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗖𝗮𝗹𝗹) • 𝗕𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗳𝗼𝗿: High-performance, low-latency distributed systems • 𝗪𝗵𝘆? gRPC leverages HTTP/2 and protocol buffers (Protobufs) for faster data transmission. It supports bidirectional streaming, making it perfect for microservices and mobile applications where speed is critical. 𝗪𝗲𝗯𝗦𝗼𝗰𝗸𝗲𝘁𝘀 • 𝗕𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗳𝗼𝗿: Real-time applications (gaming, chat, live notifications) • 𝗪𝗵𝘆? WebSockets enable persistent, two-way communication between client and server, ensuring ultra-low latency for high-interactivity scenarios. 𝗠𝗤𝗧𝗧 (𝗠𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗤𝘂𝗲𝘂𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗧𝗲𝗹𝗲𝗺𝗲𝘁𝗿𝘆 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁) • 𝗕𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗳𝗼𝗿: IoT applications • 𝗪𝗵𝘆? MQTT is a lightweight protocol designed for low-bandwidth, power-constrained devices. Its publish-subscribe model makes it perfect for sensor-based systems where efficiency is key. 𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝘁𝗼 𝗨𝘀𝗲 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁? REST → General-purpose web applications GraphQL → Dynamic data queries and front-end flexibility SOAP → Secure, enterprise-grade systems gRPC → Microservices & real-time communication WebSockets → Live, interactive applications MQTT → IoT and connected devices Choosing the right API architecture isn’t just a technical decision—it’s a 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗴𝗶𝗰 one. The right API can unlock better performance, enhance developer experience, and future-proof your application. 𝗪𝗵𝗶𝗰𝗵 𝗔𝗣𝗜 𝗱𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻 𝗱𝗼 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝘀𝘁, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗳𝗮𝘃𝗼𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗲 𝘂𝘀𝗲 𝗰𝗮𝘀𝗲𝘀? Use AutoEncoder Reconstruction (steps 👇) 🔥 More 𝗔𝗱𝘃𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗱 𝗠𝗟 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗺𝗲 here: https://lnkd.in/emb4cFCS 🧠 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗔𝘂𝘁𝗼𝗘𝗻𝗰𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗿 (𝗔𝗘) 𝗥𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗘𝗿𝗿𝗼𝗿? AutoEncoders are neural networks trained to reconstruct their input. The reconstruction error measures the difference between input and output. For anomaly detection, a model is trained on normal (anomaly-free) data. Higher reconstruction errors indicate anomalies, as the model struggles to reproduce unseen patterns. 𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝘁𝗼 𝘂𝘀𝗲 𝗔𝘂𝘁𝗼𝗘𝗻𝗰𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗿 𝗥𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗘𝗿𝗿𝗼𝗿 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗮𝗻𝗼𝗺𝗮𝗹𝘆 𝗱𝗲𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻: 1. 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝗮𝗻 𝗔𝘂𝘁𝗼𝗘𝗻𝗰𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗿: Train the AutoEncoder on clean (normal) data to learn the typical patterns. 2. 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗽𝘂𝘁𝗲 𝗥𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗘𝗿𝗿𝗼𝗿: For new data, calculate the reconstruction error (e.g., Mean Squared Error). 3. 𝗦𝗲𝘁 𝗮 𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗵𝗼𝗹𝗱 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗳𝗹𝗮𝗴 𝗮𝗻𝗼𝗺𝗮𝗹𝗶𝗲𝘀: Choose a threshold based on the error distribution from the training data (e.g., 95th percentile). 🟢 𝗔𝗱𝘃𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲𝘀: ↳ Handles high-dimensional non-linear data ↳ Learns complex relationships and patterns ↳ Handles both numerical and categorical features 🔴 𝗗𝗶𝘀𝗮𝗱𝘃𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲𝘀: ↳ Requires sufficient training set size ↳ Requires careful tuning of hyperparameters ♻️ Repost to network to show your interest in Anomaly Detection! 🔥 More 𝗔𝗱𝘃𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗱 𝗠𝗟 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗺𝗲 here: https://lnkd.in/emb4cFCS P.S. posts.title: Best ML Pipeline Practices
posts.content: Timur Bikmukhametov, PhD View Timur Bikmukhametov, PhD’s profile • 2nd Helping grow ML skills & careers in my ML Academy | World Top 3 ML LinkedIn Voice (Favikon) 1yr • 1yr Visible to everyone Data Scientists HAVE TO master ML pipelines. These DS mistakes can break ML pipelines: 1️⃣ Using ambiguous library versions 2️⃣ Ignoring model monitoring 3️⃣ Overlooking data drifts 🔴 These mistakes lead to: ↳ Non-reproducible pipelines that fail unpredictably. ↳ Inability to detect and debug performance issues. ↳ Model degradation due to unaddressed data drift. 🟢 Instead, follow these best practices: ↳ Pin library versions explicitly (e.g., scikit-learn==1.2.2) in requirements.txt or environment.yaml ↳ Track model accuracy for every prediction with your own module or using tools like Evidently, Neptune, or Weights & Biases ↳ Monitor data drift with univariate and multivariate methods with your own module or using tools like Evidently or NannyML. Don’t excuse yourself with: ↳ "The library versions don’t matter." ↳ "I’ll monitor performance later." ↳ "Data drift doesn’t impact my model." Best practices make pipelines reliable, reproducible, and scalable for production environments. ♻️ Repost to network to show your interest in ML Pipeline Best Practices! P.S. Did you use any tools that I mentioned in the post? (for more ML tutorials and resources, subscribe to my newsletter: https://lnkd.in/gddXakxh) Best ML Pipeline Practices

posts.content: Timur Bikmukhametov, PhD View Timur Bikmukhametov, PhD’s profile • 2nd Helping grow ML skills & careers in my ML Academy | World Top 3 ML LinkedIn Voice (Favikon) 1yr • 1yr Visible to everyone Simple way to smooth noise in time series (explained in 3 simple steps) 𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐄𝐱𝐩𝐨𝐧𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐚𝐥 𝐒𝐦𝐨𝐨𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐠? Exponential Smoothing reduces noise in time series data by giving exponentially decreasing weights to older observations. 🤔 𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐝𝐨𝐞𝐬 𝐢𝐭 𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐤? 1️⃣ 𝗖𝗵𝗼𝗼𝘀𝗲 𝗮 𝗦𝗺𝗼𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗣𝗮𝗿𝗮𝗺𝗲𝘁𝗲𝗿 (α) Alpha (α) controls how much weight is given to the most recent data point versus past data. -> A high α (e.g., 0.4) heavily weights recent data, adapting quickly to new changes but may retain more noise. -> A low α (e.g., 0.1) averages data over a longer period, leading to smoother curves but slower adaptation to changes. 2️⃣ 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗽𝘂𝘁𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗙𝗶𝗹𝘁𝗲𝗿 At each step, the value is calculated as: Filtered[t] = α*Original[t] + (1 - α)*Filtered[t-1] 3️⃣ 𝗙𝗶𝗻𝗲-𝘁𝘂𝗻𝗲 𝗦𝗺𝗼𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 By adjusting α, you can balance between preserving sharp changes (high α) and reducing noise (low α). 🟢 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐬: ↳ Simple to implement with minimal configuration. ↳ Ideal for real-time systems since only past data is needed. 🔴 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐬: ↳ Doesn't handle sudden change points effectively (check the gif👇). ↳ Not suitable for seasonal or cyclic data unless extended (e.g., Holt-Winters method). ♻️ Repost to your network to show your interest in time series! P.S. Which method do you use for time series noise reduction?

YData Profiling (ex-Pandas Profiling) automatise une partie de l'analyse exploratoire en générant un rapport ultra-complet en quelques lignes de code. 🔍 Ce que ça fait pour vous (entre autres): ✅ Statistiques descriptives détaillées (moyenne, médiane, valeurs manquantes…) ✅ Corrélations et relations entre variables ✅ Détection des valeurs aberrantes et doublons ✅ Analyse des données textuelles et temporelles ✅ Export en HTML interactif pour une visualisation claire Son utilisation est très simple : 𝗱𝗳 = 𝗽𝗱.𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗱_𝗰𝘀𝘃('𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮.𝗰𝘀𝘃') 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗳𝗶𝗹𝗲 = 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗳𝗶𝗹𝗲𝗥𝗲𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁(𝗱𝗳, 𝘁𝗶𝘁𝗹𝗲="𝗥𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁 𝗱𝗲 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗳𝗶𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴") 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗳𝗶𝗹𝗲.𝘁𝗼_𝗳𝗶𝗹𝗲("𝗿𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁.𝗵𝘁𝗺𝗹") ⚠️ Petit bémol : sur de très gros datasets, ça peut être un peu lent. Pensez au mode minimal pour accélérer l'analyse ! ___ 🕵️‍♂️ 𝗝𝗲 𝗳𝗮𝗶𝘀 𝗹𝗮 𝘃𝗲𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗲 𝗽𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝘃𝗼𝘂𝘀 : 15 minutes top chrono tous les mardis matins pour rester à la pointe des nouveautés en matière de data science, machine learning et IA avec ma 𝗻𝗲𝘄𝘀𝗹𝗲𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿 : lien sur mon profil ! posts.content: Gaël PENESSOT View Gaël PENESSOT’s profile • 2nd Helping data analysts boost their efficiency | Python & Data Analysis Trainer | Content Creator | BI Author 1yr • 1yr Visible to everyone Trop content de vous partager LA nouveauté qui va changer la vie des devs Streamlit ! La version 1.42 vient de sortir, et elle apporte enfin ce qu'on attendait tous : l'authentification native ! Plus besoin de bricoler des solutions maison, maintenant c'est ultra simple de protéger vos apps. Quelques lignes de code et hop, vos utilisateurs peuvent se connecter via Google, Microsoft, GitHub ou même avec un bon vieux combo email/mot de passe via Okta. Regardez comme c'est simple : import streamlit as st if not st.experimental_user.get("is_logged_in", False): if st.button("Login"): st.login("auth0") else: st.write(f"Hello, {st.experimental_user.name}!") Et le plus cool ? Ça marche avec n'importe quel fournisseur OpenID. Vous pouvez même gérer vos secrets via des variables d'environnement pour un déploiement plus flexible. posts.content: Gaël PENESSOT View Gaël PENESSOT’s profile • 2nd Helping data analysts boost their efficiency | Python & Data Analysis Trainer | Content Creator | BI Author 1yr • 1yr Visible to everyone Comment j'ai divisé par deux mon temps d'analyse exploratoire en abandonnant pandas.describe() Depuis des années, je forme des data analysts et le constat est toujours le même : nous nous contentons trop souvent des outils par défaut, sans explorer les alternatives plus performantes. Découvrez deux bibliothèques Python qui vont révolutionner votre analyse exploratoire : ▪️ Skimpy : Une version moderne et enrichie de describe() qui fonctionne aussi avec Polars. Elle offre une vue d'ensemble claire de vos données, incluant les distributions et les valeurs manquantes. ▪️ SummaryTools : Pour ceux qui veulent aller encore plus loin, avec des rapports interactifs et personnalisables. Idéal pour partager vos analyses avec vos collègues non-techniques. Ces outils m'ont permis de réduire de 50% le temps passé sur l'analyse exploratoire de mes données. Un vrai game-changer pour la productivité ! Bonus : Ces deux bibliothèques sont compatibles avec les nouveaux frameworks comme Polars, parfait pour ceux qui cherchent des alternatives plus rapides à Pandas. 🔥 Je viens de publier Baribal sur PyPI, une nouvelle bibliothèque qui apporte la puissance de la fonction glimpse() de R/dplyr et maintenant polars directement dans Pandas ! Une alternative légère et efficace pour ceux qui souhaitent garder leur workflow Pandas tout en bénéficiant des fonctionnalités modernes de Polars. Qu'en pensez-vous ? Utilisez-vous déjà ces outils dans votre travail quotidien ? Pour installer et tester : pip install skimpy summarytools baribal PS : Baribal est une espèce d'ours brun.
